title: Novel Over-the-Air Federated Learning via Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface and SWIPT
q1_support: p. 11: "we consider the Rician fading to model the small-scale fading"; custom path-loss plus Rician simulator, with no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel.
q2_support: p. 13: "the test accuracy results are obtained based on the 10 000 test samples"; a held-out part of MNIST, and no new scenario, band or configuration is used for testing (the number of devices varies only for the optimizer convergence, p. 12).
q3_support: p. 11: "Error-Free", "Random RIS Coefficients" and "Without RIS" are the benchmarks, all defined by the paper itself; no earlier published aggregation design or learned baseline is compared.
q4_support: p. 10: "the overall complexity of Algorithm 2 is given by" a big-O expression in U, M and N; p. 11: "the overall complexity of Algorithm 3 is" also given as big-O.
q5_support: p. 13: "an image identification task based on the MNIST data set"; this is a learning-task dataset only, the channel is simulated, and the paper gives no code or data link.
function: Over-the-air aggregation of local gradients via RIS-assisted AirComp, with RIS-assisted SWIPT model broadcast; joint device selection, beamforming, power splitting and RIS coefficients (p. 2-3).
system: AP with M=10 antennas, passive reflecting RIS with N=40 elements, U=10 single-antenna devices; Rician fading; no frequency band stated (p. 3, 11).
method: Federated training of a linear regression model and a fully connected MNIST network; RIS and beamformers designed by alternating optimization and SCA, not learned (p. 3, 13).
data_channel: Custom simulator: path loss with Rician fading (factors 0, 0, infinity), synthetic linear-regression data and MNIST for the learning task; no standard channel model or measurements (p. 11-13).
test_conditions: Same simulated setting for training and testing; sweeps of number of devices and SNR requirement; MNIST accuracy on 10,000 test samples; no new scenario (p. 12-14).
baselines: Error-Free ideal aggregation, Random RIS Coefficients, Without RIS; no earlier learned method or published aggregation design compared (p. 11).
metrics: Harvested power, convergence of algorithms (objective versus iterations), FL training loss for linear regression, MNIST test accuracy (p. 12-14).
complexity: Order of complexity of the DL-SWIPT and UL-AirComp algorithms in U, M, N (exponent 3.5) and iteration counts; SCA iterations plotted (p. 10-12).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Over-the-air FL (RIS plus SWIPT): the learned element is the FL model trained across devices (linear regression, MNIST), so it passes the no_learning check; the transceiver and RIS design is optimization (AO, SCA), not learned. Area 7 (over-the-air aggregation). Table I of p. 11 was read from the page image.

title: Over-the-Air Federated Learning and Optimization
function: Excluded as survey (tutorial): the paper presents itself as a tutorial. p. 1: "In this tutorial, we focus on FL via over-the-air computation (AirComp)".
first_notes: Excluded as survey (tutorial). p. 1: "In this tutorial, we focus on FL via over-the-air computation (AirComp)"; p. 23: "There are many open directions to extend this tutorial." It analyzes existing AirFedAvg variants (convergence theorems, simulations on p. 20-23). Borderline: if the reviewer reads it as a method paper, it is excluded as system, since the link is single-antenna with no RIS (p. 6: "edge server and N single-antenna edge devices"; p. 15: SISO focus; RIS only as extension, p. 18). PDF is arXiv 2310.10089v1, Over-the-Air Federated Learning and Optimization.
second_notes: Reason survey, p. 1: "In this tutorial, we focus on FL via over-the-air computation (AirComp)"; p. 2: "motivates this comprehensive tutorial on the convergence of AirFL"; p. 4 Fig. 1 "Taxonomy of this tutorial". The work analyzes the convergence of existing algorithms (p. 12: AirFedAvg-M is used in [49], [53], ...) with the COTAF denoising factor of [53]; it proposes no new aggregation or transceiver design. If the reviewer judged it a research article, the next code would be system: p. 6 "a single-antenna edge server and N single-antenna edge devices" (SISO, no RIS, area 7); multi-antenna and RIS appear only as discussed extensions (p. 15, p. 18). PDF is arXiv 2310.10089v1 with the title Over-the-Air Federated Learning and Optimization; it does not print the DOI.

title: Random Aggregate Beamforming for Over-the-Air Federated Learning in Large-Scale Networks
q1_support: p. 3: "hk ∼ CN (0, I)" - custom i.i.d. Rayleigh simulator; no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel is used anywhere in the paper.
q2_support: p. 10: "classification tasks on the well-known CIFAR10 data sets" - the beamformer is untrained and the FL model is tested only on CIFAR10; no scenario, band or dataset unseen in training is reported.
q3_support: p. 9: "Novel DC Method [31]" - earlier published OTA-FL aggregation design compared on number of selected devices (p. 10, Fig. 8) and accuracy; p. 8: "Random+DC" is a non-learned baseline compared on MSE.
q4_support: p. 3: "low, which are O(N + K log K) and O(N + K)" - complexity of the proposed scheme, derived in Sec. III-B (p. 5).
q5_support: p. 10: "classification tasks on the well-known CIFAR10 data sets" - public dataset of the learning task only; channels are simulated and no code or data link or DOI is given.
function: Joint device selection and aggregate (receive) beamforming for AirComp model aggregation in over-the-air federated learning (p. 1, 3).
system: K single-antenna devices, aggregator with N antennas (N=8 in CDF check, N=4 in FL runs, swept in Fig. 7); no RIS; frequency band not stated (p. 3, 6, 10).
method: Federated learning (ResNet18, local SGD) over AirComp; the aggregate beamformer is a random-sampling plus sorting scheme, not trained (p. 3, 5, 10).
data_channel: Synthetic i.i.d. Rayleigh channels hk~CN(0,I) (p. 3); non-i.i.d. CIFAR10 split for the FL task (p. 10); no standardized channel model or measurements.
test_conditions: No training/test channel split; Monte Carlo (1000 runs) sweeps of K, S, N and MSE threshold; CIFAR10 test accuracy for FL (p. 6, 9, 10).
baselines: Non-learned: Random+DC, Iterative (DC), l1+SDR [36]; earlier OTA-FL design: DC method of [31]; no neural-network beamforming baseline (p. 8-9).
metrics: Aggregate MSE/sigma^2, number of selected devices, and CIFAR10 test accuracy of the FL model (p. 9-10).
complexity: O(N+K log K) for MSE minimization, O(N+K) for device-count maximization; O(Nm(N+K log K)) with Nm sampled beamformers (p. 3, 5, 8).
first_notes: Include, area 7: joint device selection and aggregate beamforming for AirComp FL (p. 5, 9); the aggregator has N antennas (p. 6), so the system check passes. Caveat for the reviewer: the beamformer is random sampling, not learned, so no_learning passes only through the FL-over-the-air rule. The effect of the aggregate error on FL is simulated as retransmission with probability 1-exp(-a MSE/sigma^2) (p. 27). q3 rests on [24] as the earlier published aggregation design, which is optimization-based. PDF is arXiv 2403.18946v1, same title, formatted as IEEE TWC.
published_notes: Included under the over-the-air FL rule: the learned element is the FL model (ResNet18 on CIFAR10, p. 10), while the proposed beamformer is a non-learned random-sampling scheme (p. 5). Area 7 because the problem is the aggregation itself (aggregate beamforming and device selection, p. 1). q3 rests on [31] as the earlier published aggregation design; Random+DC and Iterative are the paper's own heuristics and do not count as the learned baseline (p. 8). The aggregator has N>1 antennas, so the system check passes.

title: Multi-UAV Hierarchical Intelligent Traffic Offloading Network Optimization Based on Deep Federated Learning
function: Excluded as above_phy: the learned agent chooses UAV flight (angle, speed, altitude) and the traffic offloading share, with fixed transmit power, so no physical-layer function (p. 5).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Reason above_phy: the action space is the UAV flight and the offloaded share of traffic, p. 5: "Action decisions include UAV flight decisions and the task size of handling traffic offloading". Transmit powers are fixed inputs in Table I (p. 4). Federated learning averages model weights digitally at the leader UAV (p. 7-8), and CPRAFT is a leader-election consensus (p. 8). No channel estimation, detection, beamforming or power control is learned. Table I of p. 4 was read from the page image.
second_notes: Title and DOI 10.1109/JIOT.2024.3363188 are on p. 1, so the PDF is the paper of the DOI. Reason above_phy, p. 5: the action is A = {FUAV(t), Dn(t)}, where "FUAV (t) includes the UAV's flight angle, horizontal flight rate and flight altitude, and Dn (t) indicates the proportion of traffic offloaded to UAVs offloading tasks", and the reward is the negative delay and energy cost of computation offloading (p. 5, Eq. 16). The learning therefore performs task offloading and UAV trajectory/placement decisions, both listed as above the physical layer; no transmit power, beam, or radio resource is learned, so the aerial-link exception does not apply. The federated learning is digital FedAvg at the leader UAV (p. 8, Eq. 36), not over-the-air computation, and the CPRAFT part is a consensus protocol for leader election (pp. 8-9).

title: Energy-Efficient Power Control for Multiple-Task Split Inference in UAVs: A Tiny Learning-Based Approach
function: Excluded as above_phy: the learned agent selects the transmission mode, whether to use split inference (p. 1, 5-6); power is set by optimization (p. 7-8).
first_notes: Excluded as above_phy. The learned part (DDQN, tiny RL) only chooses between direct transmission and split inference: p. 1: "discrete transmission modes for sequential tasks"; p. 6: "outputs the decision of transmission mode at each time slot" (action space of size 2). This is an edge computing decision. Transmit power is not learned: p. 8: "Obtain the transmit power according to equation (28)", a closed-form KKT solution with SAA and ADMM (p. 6-7). The aerial-link exception of above_phy is not applied, since the learned output is the mode and not power. If the reviewer reads no_learning as also covering this case, the code would be no_learning. PDF is arXiv 2401.00445v1, same title.
second_notes: Reason above_phy. p. 2: "TRL-based approach is utilized to determine whether split inference should be employed for processing tasks"; p. 6: action space of size 2, the transmission mode (direct transmission of raw data or computation-transmission of the feature map). The physical-layer decision, transmit power, is not learned: p. 9 "OP is used to optimize the transmit power in each time slot", solved in closed form by KKT (Theorem 1, p. 7) and ADMM over SAA samples (p. 8), so the clause on learned power control in aerial links does not apply. The baselines are "offloading policies" (p. 8). The UAV-to-server channel is a scalar coefficient g_t (p. 3), so the link is single-antenna. PDF is arXiv 2401.00445v1, Energy-Efficient Power Control for Multiple-Task Split Inference in UAVs: A Tiny Learning-Based Approach; it does not print the DOI.

title: DRL-Optimized Optical Communication for a Reliable UAV-Based Maritime Data Transmission
q1_support: p. 9: "we simulate different wave scenarios based on the Tessendorf algorithm"; the optical channel is the paper's own Lambertian model (p. 4), and the measured Weihai buoy data give drift positions only, not a channel.
q2_support: p. 12: "We leave further exploration of this topic for future research"; sim-to-real transfer is only discussed, and the wave heights 0.3 to 1.2 m of p. 9 are not stated as unseen in training.
q3_support: p. 10: "we compare the angular error during adjustment with the performance of the PID controller"; p. 11: "compared the average SNR with the DDPG-based scheme" (DDPG applied to the same angle control problem).
q4_support: p. 9: "the SAC is implemented by Python 3.9 to simulate using the open source module Stable Baselines3"; no order of complexity, operations, parameters or runtime of the method is reported anywhere.
q5_support: p. 9: "2020 Weihai offshore buoy observation data set provided by the Marine Science Data Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences"; third-party buoy drift positions, not a channel or signal data set, and no own code or data link.
function: SAC reinforcement learning adjusts the buoy LED transmitter rotation angle (beam pointing) toward the UAV under waves; UAV repositioning uses SARIMA prediction and LQR, not learned (p. 4-8).
system: Single LED transmitter on buoy, single photodetector on UAV, LOS optical IM/DD with OOK, no RIS; band not stated beyond 100 nm spectrum width (p. 4, 9).
method: Soft actor-critic reinforcement learning, trained by simulation episodes on Tessendorf wave dynamics; sim-to-real fine-tuning is only discussed, not performed (p. 6-7, 12).
data_channel: Custom optical channel simulator (Lambertian LED, path loss, ambient-light AWGN) with Tessendorf-generated waves; real 2020 Weihai buoy observation data used for drift prediction (p. 3-4, 9).
test_conditions: Training and test conditions not separated: results at maximum wave heights 0.3 to 1.2 m and several UAV altitudes; no unseen scenario or adaptation stated (p. 9-11).
baselines: Non-learned: PID controller; learned: DDPG for angle control, LSTM for buoy position prediction; ablated variants (p. 10-12).
metrics: Angle adjustment error versus target angle, received light intensity, average SNR, energy consumption, MAE/RMSE/SSE of position prediction (p. 10-12).
complexity: none
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Area 6 proposed: SAC learns beam pointing of an optical UAV-buoy link (an aerial link), so the single-aperture link is admitted as NTN; reviewer to confirm that this link counts as area 6. UAV position prediction uses SARIMA and LQR, not learned (p. 7-8). The real Weihai buoy data (p. 9) give buoy drift positions for the position predictor, while the SAC angle and state come from Tessendorf waves (p. 6-7), so q1 and q5 are proposed as 0; reviewer to confirm. Tables II and IV read from page images (p. 9-10).

title: Deep Learning Methods for Secure IoT SWIPT Networks
q1_support: p. 4: "The Rician factor is assumed to be KR = 3 dB"; custom path-loss plus Rician simulator, with no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel.
q2_support: p. 20: "The current DL model is tailored for specific node-antenna configurations"; the sweeps over L and K (p. 14) do not state a model trained at one configuration and tested at another.
q3_support: p. 12: "compare the results of DQN, DNN (without the inclusion of Q-learning), SCA [23], SDP [24], and DDQN algorithms [26]"; harvested energy and secrecy capacity are compared (p. 13).
q4_support: p. 19: "the proposed DQN with the approximate complexity bound" O of the sum of N(l-1)N(l); Table III (p. 20) lists the SCA and SDP complexity bounds.
q5_support: p. 12: "we generated a set of channel state information"; the channel data are simulated, and the paper gives no code or data link.
function: DQN outputs the HAP transmit beamforming vectors maximizing the minimum harvested energy under secrecy capacity and power constraints, for consolidated and split signal cases (p. 6, 8-9).
system: Hybrid access point with N_T=10 antennas, L=3 single-antenna EH nodes, one single-antenna ID receiver, K=4 two-antenna eavesdroppers; Rician fading; no RIS; band not stated (p. 4, 12).
method: DQN: Q-learning with a fully connected DNN (hidden layers of 120 and 60 nodes), reinforcement training with Adam on simulated CSI; one agent (p. 11-12).
data_channel: Custom simulated channel: path-loss exponent 3, Rician fading (K-factor 3 dB), norm-bounded CSI errors, generated randomly per episode; no standard model or measurement (p. 4, 7, 14).
test_conditions: Random channel draws per training episode; sweeps of maximum transmit power, EH nodes L and eavesdroppers K; model tailored to specific node-antenna configurations (p. 14, 20).
baselines: SCA [23] and SDP [24] optimization (non-learned); DNN without Q-learning, DDQN [26] and D3QN (learned) (p. 12-14).
metrics: Harvested energy, secrecy capacity, power efficiency, energy efficiency, cumulative reward, convergence versus iterations (p. 13-19).
complexity: Big-O complexity O(sum of N_{l-1}N_l over layers) for the DQN compared with SCA and SDP bounds in Table III (p. 19-20).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Area 3: the DQN action is the HAP transmit beamforming vector (p. 9), a multi-antenna precoder; the secrecy and energy harvesting objectives do not change the function. Tables II and III (p. 12, 20) read from page images.

title: RIS-Assisted UAV-Enabled Green Communications for Industrial IoT Exploiting Deep Learning
q1_support: p. 5: "they follow Rayleigh fading with path loss taken into consideration"; own Rician (RIS links, p. 4) and Rayleigh simulator, no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 13: "To verify the generalization ability of the algorithm, we consider different UAV’s flying altitudes"; the training altitude is never stated (Table II: 10^4 training, 10^3 testing samples), so a held-out test or retraining per altitude is not excluded.
q3_support: p. 12: "we can use exhaustive search to find the optimal solution"; baselines are exhaustive search, random power/phase and no RIS; the only learned schemes are the paper's own variants, so no earlier learned baseline.
q4_support: p. 13: "are 314.20, 68.18, and 92.37, respectively" (seconds to compute and plot the Fig. 13 curves for the optimum, centralized DNN and distributed DNN); measured runtime only.
q5_support: p. 11: "empirical channel models are exploited to train the DNNs"; channels come from the authors' own simulator, with no code or data link, no public dataset and no availability statement.
function: Unsupervised DNNs jointly choose D2D transmit power, cellular channel allocation and discrete RIS phase shifts to maximize D2D energy efficiency in a UAV-served network (pp. 3, 7-8).
system: Single-antenna UAV aerial BS, CUEs and D2D pairs; passive reflecting RIS, M=4 elements, 3-bit phases (L=8), amplitude 1; frequency band not stated (pp. 4, 11).
method: Fully connected DNNs (power, channel, RIS modules with softmax outputs, optional dropout) trained offline, unsupervised with penalty loss and Adam; centralized and distributed variants (pp. 3, 8-10).
data_channel: Simulated CSI: Rician for RIS links, Rayleigh with path loss for the others; 10^4 training and 10^3 testing samples (pp. 4-5, 12).
test_conditions: Default UAV at 30 m, K=2, D=3, M=4; test sweeps over M (4-64) and UAV altitude (30-380 m); training conditions of the sweeps not stated (pp. 11-13).
baselines: Non-learned: exhaustive-search optimum, max-power/random-phase, random-power/random-phase, no RIS. No earlier learned method; only own variants (centralized with/without dropout, distributed) (p. 12).
metrics: Energy efficiency of D2D users (bits/Hz/Joule), training loss and EE versus learning rate, computation time (pp. 12-13).
complexity: Total time to compute Fig. 13 curves on Intel i5-12500 CPU: optimum 314.20 s, centralized DNN 68.18 s, distributed DNN 92.37 s; no operation or parameter counts (p. 13).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Area 6 by the specificity order (aerial UAV BS, learned power and channel resource control plus RIS phases); area 3 (RIS phase shifts) also fits and is the alternative. Single-antenna links but a RIS is present, so the system check passes. q2 is borderline: the altitude sweep is called a generalization test (p. 13) but the training altitude is not stated. q4 rests on a coarse measured total runtime.

title: Blockchain-Based Trustworthy and Efficient Hierarchical Federated Learning for UAV-Enabled IoT Networks
q1_support: p. 4: "A realistic channel model considering both LOS and NLOS component is utilized to capture the ground-to-air (G2A) channel [36]"; own LoS/NLOS pathloss with i.i.d. CN(0,1) fading, no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 9: "The number of EDs ranges from 30 to 120 to manifest the effectiveness of our proposed scheme"; a parameter sweep only, with no statement that a trained policy is tested on conditions unseen in training.
q3_support: p. 9: "EDs randomly form clusters and connect to UAVs without considering the communication link and data distribution" (Random baseline); the four baselines are association schemes, none an earlier learned power or deployment method.
q4_support: p. 6: "to achieve low-complexity device-cluster matching"; qualitative only, with no complexity order, operation or parameter count, or runtime for the SAC or the greedy step.
q5_support: p. 8: "are adopted to train the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and verify the proposed scheme" (CIFAR-10, MNIST); learning-task datasets do not count, channels are own simulation, and no code or data link is given.
function: Soft actor-critic DRL jointly sets device and UAV transmit power, device CPU frequency and UAV positions to trade FL learning latency against data-distribution distance (pp. 6-7).
system: Single-antenna ground devices upload to hovering UAVs with K=4 antennas (virtual MIMO); air-to-air UAV links; 2 GHz carrier, 1 MHz bandwidth; no RIS (pp. 3-4, 9).
method: Soft actor-critic DRL (five networks, entropy regularization, replay buffer) for power, CPU frequency and UAV deployment, alternating with non-learned greedy device association; hierarchical FL trains CNNs (pp. 6-8).
data_channel: Own air-ground simulator: probabilistic LoS/NLOS pathloss [36], i.i.d. CN(0,1) small-scale fading, free-space air-to-air; FL data CIFAR-10 and MNIST; devices random in 1000 m square (pp. 4, 8).
test_conditions: SAC training and test conditions are not described; results swept over 30-120 devices, per-cluster power 0-2 W and energy budget 60-140 J (pp. 9-11).
baselines: Ideal (unlimited resources), Random association, HierFedAvg, ELASTIC: association or selection schemes; none described as a learned power or deployment method (p. 9).
metrics: Global model accuracy and learning utility (weighted learning latency and data distance) versus epochs, number of devices, per-cluster power and energy budget (pp. 9-11).
complexity: none; only a qualitative low-complexity remark on greedy association (p. 6).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Borderline inclusion: FL aggregation is digital, so not area 7. The SAC learns transmit power of aerial links (physical layer under the aerial rule, p. 7 action space) jointly with UAV deployment and CPU frequency, so it passes above_phy and fits area 6. If the reviewer reads the FL latency objective as above the physical layer, exclude as above_phy. Device association is greedy and non-learned.

title: Transformer-Based Predictive Beamforming for Integrated Sensing and Communication in Vehicular Networks
q1_support: p. 4: "a line-of-sight (LOS) channel is employed [34]"; own LOS model with path-loss exponent 2.55 (Table II, p. 10), no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 10: "each simulation result is the average of 200 samples run on the test set"; a held-out part of the same data, and the sweeps over power, antennas, noise and distance (pp. 11-13) never state a different training condition.
q3_support: p. 10: "convolutional LSTM network (HCL-Net) for predictive beamforming [27]" is the earlier learned baseline and "The random beamforming scheme is utilized" the non-learned one; both compared on sum rate (Fig. 6).
q4_support: p. 11: "in terms of parameters, FlOPs, and FPS"; Table III gives ECT-Net 0.10M parameters and 2.70M FLOPs, and Eqs. 21-22 (p. 9) give the Big-O orders.
q5_support: p. 10: "data sets is 2000, divided into the training set"; data come from the authors' own simulation, with no code or data link and no public dataset.
function: Convolution-Transformer ECT-Net predicts the next-instant ISAC transmit beamforming matrix from the previous echoes and beamformer, maximizing communication sum rate under a sensing SINR constraint (pp. 5-8).
system: mmWave massive-MIMO RSU, Nt=64 transmit and Nr=16 receive antennas on separate full-duplex ULAs, K=12 single-antenna vehicles, LOS channel, 30 GHz; no RIS (pp. 3, 9-10).
method: Two CNN modules plus attention encoder with residual link (ECT-Net), trained offline unsupervised with a penalty loss, validated, then used for online prediction (pp. 6-9).
data_channel: Own simulation: LOS mmWave channel, path-loss exponent 2.55, kinematic vehicle motion (20 m/s, 0.1 s); 2000 samples split 8:1:1 into training, validation, testing (pp. 4-5, 10).
test_conditions: Test on held-out 10% of the same simulated data (200 samples); sweeps over power, antennas 8-36, vehicles, speed, noise, road distance; no train/test mismatch stated (pp. 10-13).
baselines: Non-learned: random beamforming. Learned: HCL-Net convolutional LSTM [27]. Noise-free upper bound is the proposed network without noise; plain Transformer only in complexity table (pp. 10-11).
metrics: Average achievable communication sum rate (bits/s/Hz), average minimum sensing SINR, parameters, FLOPs, FPS, training epochs (pp. 10-14).
complexity: Big-O orders of offline training and online prediction (Eqs. 21-22); ECT-Net 0.10M parameters, 2.70M FLOPs, 930.7 FPS versus HCL-Net 0.86M, 1.12M, 422.6 (pp. 9, 11).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Beamforming for ISAC from echoes, so area 5. q3: the noise-free upper bound is a variant of the proposed network, and the plain Transformer [29] appears only in the complexity table (Table III), so HCL-Net [27] and random beamforming carry the criterion. q2: the ECT-Net input and output sizes change with the antenna number (p. 8), and no train/test mismatch is stated for any sweep.

title: Deep Compression for Efficient and Accelerated Over-the-Air Federated Learning
q1_support: p. 7: "has Rayleigh fading effect with i.i.d. gains on the transmitted GVs"; own Rayleigh plus AWGN simulation with a free-space path-loss term (Table II), no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 7: "We then observe the effects of varying SNR on the accuracy of uncompressed ResNet50 and corresponding compressed versions of ResNet50"; a sweep with convergence curves per setting (Figs. 10-13), and no trained model is tested on unseen conditions.
q3_support: p. 7: "the accuracy of the model is termed as UC accuracy/ideal accuracy"; the only reference is the uncompressed model and the paper's own variants, with no earlier published compression or aggregation design compared.
q4_support: p. 13: "calculate the energy requirements for addition and multiplication operations for various models"; sizes, operation counts and energy (Tables II, III, V) are costs of the models being trained, not of an aggregation or transceiver design.
q5_support: p. 7: "We utilize MNIST and CIFAR-10 data sets to train ResNet50 and InceptionV3 DNNs"; learning-task datasets do not count, the channel is simulated, and no code or data link is given.
function: Over-the-air aggregation of model updates of pruned and quantized DNNs from many devices by analog superposition over a Rayleigh fading channel with AWGN (pp. 4, 6-7).
system: One parameter server, E=50 or 100 edge devices at 50 m; OFDM subchannels, 20 MHz bandwidth, 2.4 GHz center frequency; antenna configuration not stated; no RIS (p. 7).
method: Magnitude pruning (30/50/70%) and quantization-aware training (FP16, INT8) with fine-tuning on ResNet50 and InceptionV3, trained by federated averaging with SGD, supervised classification (pp. 4-7).
data_channel: MNIST and CIFAR-10, i.i.d. partition; simulated Rayleigh fading with i.i.d. gains, AWGN, path loss at 2.4 GHz; average SNR up to 10 dB (pp. 7, 9).
test_conditions: Each setting trains an FL model (up to 1000 epochs), tested on the dataset test split: E=50 or 100, SNR 5 or 10 dB, SNR sweep (pp. 7-11).
baselines: Uncompressed model as ideal reference, plus the paper's own pruned, quantized and combined variants; no earlier compression or aggregation design compared (pp. 7-8, 12).
metrics: Test accuracy, model size (MB), convergence epochs, OTA acceleration factor (size ratio times convergence ratio), theoretical operation energy and power (pp. 8-14).
complexity: Model sizes in MB (Table III), parameters and OFDM frames of uncompressed models (Table II), multiplication and addition counts with energy (Table V); no aggregation cost (pp. 7-8, 14).
first_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match. Borderline inclusion: the contribution is compression of the models aggregated over the air (analog superposition over Rayleigh plus AWGN, no designed transceiver or power control), so area 7 holds only if OTA-FL efficiency counts as the aggregation problem; otherwise exclude as function. q4 is borderline: Table V (p. 14) lists multiplication and addition counts and energy of the compressed models, treated as the cost of the trained model under the OTA-FL rule.

title: Model Compression by Count Sketch for Over-the-Air Stateless Federated Learning

The learned PAEnet (ESnet, PRnet, Funet) estimates delay and Doppler indices of target UAVs under impulse noise. p. 1: "communication waveform-based UAV sensing situation", so OTFS is only the probing waveform. p. 5: "OTFS signal and process the echo signal reflected by the" UAV, so the UAV is a passive target and no communication receiver is modeled. p. 10: "the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm for delay Doppler" parameter estimation. pp. 10-11 report only NMSE and a detection rate (p. 11: "The detection rate, defined as the condition where the errors" are below 1); there is no BER, rate or other communication metric. This is sensing alone in a system that does not communicate. If the reviewer reads the OTFS communication waveform as making the system communicate, the nearest area would be 4, but the target is sensing, not data channel estimation or detection, and the method designs no ISAC beam, waveform or resource (area 5).

The learned PAEnet (attention residual CNN ESnet, LSTM PRnet, MLP Funet) performs radar sensing of target UAVs: p. 1 "we consider an OTFS communication waveform-based UAV sensing situation"; p. 3 "An ESnet is constructed to extract the delay and Doppler parameters for UAV sensing"; p. 5 "BS-1 and BS-2 ... transmit the OTFS signal and process the echo signal reflected by the UAV individually" and "the symbol sent at the radar detector is known"; p. 7 "OTFS waveform-based radar detection". The UAVs are non-cooperative targets (p. 1: "passive detection of unknown UAVs via communication signals"); no communication receiver, data detection, or communication metric is modeled, and results are NMSE of target delay/Doppler indices and detection rate against LS, LMMSE, CNN, and CA-CFAR (pp. 10-12). Communication appears only as motivation (Fig. 1, p. 2) and as the origin of the waveform. Not area 4, because the DD-domain estimate is of target echo parameters (range and velocity), not of a communication channel or of data symbols; not area 5, because no beam, waveform, or resource is designed; not area 6, because no UAV link is controlled. function: Learns BS beamformers for common and private messages, discrete RIS phase shifts, common-rate allocation and transmit power to maximize energy efficiency in a multi-RIS-aided RSMA downlink (p. 1-4).
system: Downlink MISO RSMA: BS with M=8 antennas, K single-antenna users, L=3 passive RISs with N elements and 2-bit discrete phases; frequency band not stated (p. 2, 4).
method: GNN on a graph of RIS, private-user and common-user nodes (D=3, q=128) with a power-control network; unsupervised, loss is negative EE plus a rate-constraint penalty (p. 3-4).

first_notes: Preprint arXiv:2405.00391v2 of LWC letter 'Beamforming Inferring by Conditional WGAN-GP for Holographic Antenna Arrays'. RIS appears only as future work (p. 5). Figs. 7-8 vary spacing and antenna number 1, but the paper does not say a trained model is reused across them, so q2 = 0.

Table I and Figs. 6-8 were read from the page images (pp. 4-5). q1 and q5 rest on WAIR-D [14], a public channel dataset that the paper describes as built on practical scenario maps and contrasts with DeepMIMO; the paper does not itself say ray tracing, so the reviewer should confirm that it counts as another public ray-tracing dataset. title: Unsupervised Learning for Joint Beamforming Design in RIS-Aided ISAC Systems

q2_support: p. 4: "100 samples are used to evaluate the generalization capability of the model"; these are held-out samples of the same Rician setting, and no unseen scenario is reported.
q3_support: p. 4: "we compare it against two representative algorithms"; both (AO, Rotation) are non-learned, and no earlier learned method for the same function is compared.
q4_support: p. 5: "the running times of the proposed method and the benchmarks are shown in Table II"; the same section gives the operation count and the order O(N^2 + N^2 log2 N + M).

system: 8-antenna ISAC base station, one single-antenna user, one sensed target, passive reflecting RIS with 32 elements; frequency band not stated (p. 1, p. 4).
method: Lightweight CNN (IBF-Net, depthwise-pointwise convolutions) trained with unsupervised learning; loss from channel correlation and sensing channel gain (p. 3).
data_channel: Simulated Rician channels similar to [11]; 500,000 generated training samples and 100 test samples (p. 4).
test_conditions: Same Rician setting for training and testing (100 test samples); RIS size N, power and threshold are varied, with no stated reuse of a model across settings (p. 4).
baselines: Non-learned only: AO, SDR-based alternating optimization [4], and Rotation, subspace rotation [7]; no learned baseline compared (p. 4).
metrics: Sensing SNR, communication SNR against the user threshold, training loss, and average running time per sample (p. 4-5).
complexity: Operation count 1184N^2+576(N^2-N)+2048N^2 log2 N+6M, O(N^2+N^2 log2 N+M); runtime 3.9 ms versus AO 6.61e3 ms at N=32 (p. 5).
openness: Code released at https://github.com/Yejacky456/DL-Beamforming-RIS-ISAC; no dataset link (p. 1).
first_notes: Preprint arXiv:2403.17324v2. Area 5: beamforming in an RIS-aided ISAC system (the transmit beamformer is closed form, Theorem 1 on p. 2; the learned network designs the RIS phases). Rotation [7] is a gradient-descent method, not learned, so q3 = 0. The GitHub link was not opened. Sweeps of RIS size in Fig. 4 are not stated to reuse one trained model, and the network depends on N (p. 3).
published_notes: Area 5 over 3: the learned RIS phases serve a joint sensing and communication beamforming problem in an ISAC system (p. 1). The transmit beamformer is the closed-form Theorem 1 (p. 2). The network input is 4xNxN and its depth depends on N (p. 3), so the sweep of N in Fig. 4 (p. 4) is not stated as testing a model on a size it was not trained for. Learned works [8]-[12] appear only in the introduction (p. 1).

title: ISAC Receiver Design: A Learning-Based Two-Stage Joint Data-and-Target Parameter Estimation
q1_support: p. 3: "Attenuation is randomly generated as a rayleigh fading style"; custom simulator with random delays and steering vectors, no 3GPP, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel is mentioned.
q2_support: p. 4: "followed by a multiplication of a random float number between [0.9, 1.1]"; this is a 10% CSI error on the same simulated channel (Fig. 4 legend: 10% CSI estimation error), with no new scenario, antennas, band or dataset.
q3_support: p. 4: "our STransformer outperforms SBRNN for both perfect and imperfect CSI, while outperforming LS when CSI is imperfect"; LS detection is non-learned, SBRNN is an earlier learned detector, compared on SER in Fig. 4.
q4_support: p. 4: "complexity of O(4 ∗ nd 2 ), while the 2-direction bi-LSTM has a time complexity of O(2 ∗ n 2 d )"; Table I on p. 4 also gives training and processing times.
q5_support: p. 3: "Simulations are done to a set of data symbols randomly generated from a normal distribution"; synthetic data, and no code or data link or public dataset appears anywhere in the letter.
function: Symbol detection (QPSK) in an uplink ISAC SIMO-OFDM receiver with a learned sliding Transformer; target AOA and delay then come from LS plus MUSIC, not learned. p. 1
system: SIMO-OFDM uplink ISAC, BS with Nr=8 antennas (ULA), UE with Nt=1, M=64 subcarriers, static target; no RIS; carrier frequency not stated. p. 3
method: Sliding Transformer (4 encoder layers, one head, ReZero, no positional encoding) classifying QPSK symbols; supervised, cross-entropy loss, trained from scratch for each SNR. p. 2
data_channel: Custom simulation: random QPSK symbols, Rayleigh-style random attenuation, random delays and steering vectors from a normal distribution; no standard or measured channel. p. 3
test_conditions: Train and test on the same channel realisations, then test with CSI differing up to 10% (random factor in [0.9, 1.1]); one model trained per SNR. p. 4
baselines: Learned: SBRNN (Bi-LSTM sliding detector), also pre-trained with transfer learning for convergence tests. Classical: LS channel-estimation-based symbol detection. p. 4
metrics: Symbol error rate versus SNR; training samples and training time to reach 90% accuracy; processing time; AOA error (degrees) and time-delay error (m) versus SNR. p. 4
complexity: Order O(4nd^2) for the Transformer versus O(2n^2d) for Bi-LSTM; Table I, Transformer vs SBRNN: training 142 vs 351 s, processing 0.023 vs 0.006 s. p. 4
first_notes: PDF is the IEEE accepted author's version (watermark p. 1), given as preprint. Area 1: only symbol detection is learned; AOA and delay use LS plus MUSIC (p. 3), not learned, so area 5 (ISAC receiver) is the alternative for the reviewer. The only train-test mismatch is the 10% CSI perturbation (p. 4), treated as CSI error; the paper calls it a generalisation test (p. 5). Fig. 4 SNR axis spans -30 to 10 dB (read from page image).
published_notes: Area 1 because the learned part is symbol detection; sensing (AOA, delay) uses LS plus MUSIC, which is not learned, so area 5 (beams, waveforms, resources) does not apply. Table I values read from the page image (p. 4). The title and DOI on p. 1 match the work.

title: GNN-Based Channel Estimation for Intelligent Reflecting Surface Aided Multiuser Systems Relying on User Locations
q1_support: p. 3: "The direct channel hd,k is assumed to follow Rayleigh fading" and "We assume the Rician fading model"; custom simulator, with no 3GPP, DeepMIMO, or measured data mentioned.
q2_support: p. 5: "we test the trained GNN under different uplink transmit power", an SNR sweep; no other scenario, array size, band, or dataset is tested, and the text does not say whether the beta=20 dB case was retrained.
q3_support: p. 3: "other DL schemes such as FNN and CNN" and "the non-DL approach, i.e., LMMSE [11]"; p. 5: "outperforms other channel estimation schemes under low pilot overhead" (NMSE).
q4_support: p. 5: "The required FLOPs of the S aggregation and combination layers in (8)" and the order O(.) of the GNN, FNN, and CNN are given as formulas.
q5_support: p. 4: "we generate 10000 samples and 1000 samples to train and test the neural networks"; data come from the authors' own simulator, and no code or data link or public dataset is given.
function: p. 1-3: Channel estimation: a GNN maps received pilot signals, plus user locations, to the cascaded user-IRS-BS channels of an IRS-aided uplink system.
system: p. 2-3: Uplink multiuser MISO, BS with M=16 antennas, K=4 single-antenna users, passive reflecting IRS with N=80 elements; carrier frequency/band not stated.
method: p. 3-4: Graph neural network with FNN aggregation and combination layers (S=2), trained offline and supervised by an MSE loss against true cascaded channels; Adam.
data_channel: p. 3-4: Custom simulator: Rayleigh direct channel, Rician IRS channels (β=30 dB), cited path-loss formulas; 10000 training and 1000 test samples; no standard or measured data.
test_conditions: p. 3, 5: Same simulated setup (M=16, K=4, N=80) for training and testing; trained at Pu=10 dBm, tested at other powers (Fig. 6); also imperfect user locations, β=20 dB.
baselines: p. 3: Non-learned LMMSE [11]; learned FNN and CNN applied to the same estimation problem; GNN without user locations (ablation) and with imperfect locations.
metrics: p. 3-5: Normalized MSE (NMSE) of the estimated cascaded channels versus pilot overhead and uplink transmit power; training-epoch convergence (Fig. 4).
complexity: p. 5: FLOPs order of GNN, FNN, and CNN given as closed-form O(.) expressions; the GNN is stated to be less complex than the FNN; no runtime.
first_notes: Included, area 2: the learned function is channel estimation of an IRS-aided link; user locations are an input feature, so this is not localization. Frequency band is never stated. The FNN and CNN baselines are the authors' own implementations of standard architectures (Tables I and II, p. 4), counted as learned baselines. Path-loss formulas are cited from refs [10], [11], not stated to come from 3GPP. q2 stays 0 because Fig. 6 (p. 4) only sweeps the transmit power of a model trained at 10 dBm, and Fig. 5 shows a beta=20 dB curve without saying whether the model was retrained; the reviewer may want to check this point.

title: Learning-Based Block-Wise Planar Channel Estimation for Time-Varying MIMO OFDM
q1_support: p. 4: "we use the CDL-B channel model [16]" for training and testing; reference [16] on p. 5 is 3GPP TR 38.901.
q2_support: p. 4: "For testing, we use the CDL-B channel with 129 ns r.m.s. delay spread and mobile speed of 100 km/h"; both lie inside the training ranges, and only the SNR extends beyond (4-18 dB versus 4-14 dB), which is an SNR sweep. No other scenario, array size or user number is tested.
q3_support: p. 4: "ICINet [11], LDAMP [13], LTMP [14], 2DU [18], 3DFF [18], LS, 2 × 1D LMMSE, 1D LMMSE" are the learned and non-learned baselines, compared on NMSE (p. 4: "Fig. 5 shows the channel estimation MSE against SNR").
q4_support: p. 4: "the complex multiplications number is (12170 + 30T )TP NMK /4"; p. 5: "the computational complexity of LBPCE is reduced by more than one order of magnitude compared with LDAMP".
q5_support: p. 4: "For the network training, we use the CDL-B channel model [16]"; channels are generated from a 3GPP model, not a public dataset or measured data, and the letter gives no code or data link.
function: Channel estimation for time-varying frequency-selective uplink MIMO-OFDM: BPCM-based LMMSE gives coarse estimates, then a 3D dilated residual CNN denoises and interpolates over time, frequency, and antennas. p. 1
system: Uplink multiuser MIMO-OFDM, BS with M=64 antennas, K=24 single-antenna users, N=48 subcarriers at 30 kHz spacing, T=28 symbols (8 pilots); no RIS; carrier frequency not stated. p. 4
method: LMMSE on a block-wise planar channel model followed by a 3D dilated residual CNN (3D-DRCN); supervised offline training with L1 loss and Adam, learning rate 1e-4. p. 4
data_channel: 3GPP TR 38.901 CDL-B simulated channels; training with 100-300 ns delay spread, 80-120 km/h, SNR 4-14 dB; testing with 129 ns, 100 km/h, SNR 4-18 dB. p. 4
test_conditions: Test on CDL-B with 129 ns and 100 km/h, inside the training ranges (100-300 ns, 80-120 km/h); test SNR 4-18 dB, training 4-14 dB. p. 4
baselines: Learned: CE-DNN, CE-CNN, SF-CNN, Model2, ICINet, LDAMP, LTMP, 2DU, 3DFF. Classical: LS, 1D LMMSE, 2x1D LMMSE; ablation: Module A without the network. p. 4
metrics: NMSE versus SNR; number of complex multiplications versus number of users. p. 4
complexity: Counts complex multiplications: module A, (NT/VU)^3+6K(NTP/VU)^2+3KUVM(NTP/VU); module B, (12170+30T)TP*N*M*K/4; over one order below LDAMP, nearly three below LTMP. p. 4-5
first_notes: Preprint arXiv:2405.11218v1. Area 2: channel estimation, where the 3D-DRCN refines block-wise planar LMMSE estimates. Test delay spread (129 ns) and speed (100 km/h) lie inside the training ranges, and only the SNR range extends (4-18 dB versus 4-14 dB), so q2 = 0. Module A is an ablation of the proposed method, not counted as the baseline. Fig. 5b varies users for complexity only, not for NMSE. No code or data link found in the text.
published_notes: Included, area 2: the learned 3D-DRCN refines the channel estimates, while module A is classical LMMSE. CDL-B comes from 3GPP TR 38.901 (reference [16], p. 5). Test delay spread and speed fall inside the training ranges, so q2 is 0. The title and DOI on p. 1 match the work.

title: Federated Learning-Based Channel Estimation for RIS-Aided Communication Systems
q1_support: p. 4: "Channel data for users in each region are generated based on the available DeepMIMO dataset" with ray-tracing scenarios; Section II (p. 2) writes a Saleh-Valenzuela model, but the data come from DeepMIMO.
q2_support: p. 4: "80% of the overall sample is devoted to model training", a split of the same DeepMIMO data and the same three regions; no other scenario, band, array size, or users are tested, and the SNR sweep does not count.
q3_support: p. 4: "LS algorithm [20], minimum mean squared error (MMSE) algorithm [5], CL-based NN [9], FL-based NN [11]"; p. 5: "improved by approximately 2.5 dB" over the CL-based NN in NMSE (Fig. 6).
q4_support: p. 4: "we have PNN = 2171456 and PHNet = 2193536", the number of parameters of the proposed HNet, with the formula for HReNet in (8).
q5_support: p. 4: "Channel data for users in each region are generated based on the available DeepMIMO dataset" [21], a public channel dataset; no code or data of its own is released.
function: p. 2-3: Channel estimation: FL-trained hierarchical networks (region classifier plus per-region estimators) map the received pilot signal to the cascaded BS-RIS-user channel of a downlink RIS-aided cell.
system: p. 2, 4: Downlink FDD single-cell; BS with M=16 (4x4) UPA antennas, reflecting RIS with N=64 (8x8) elements, R=3 regions with Kr=3 users each; frequency band not stated.
method: p. 3-4: Federated learning (parameters aggregated at the BS) of convolutional HNet and residual HReNet, each with a region classifier and per-region estimators; supervised training.
data_channel: p. 4: DeepMIMO O1 ray-tracing data, users in three regions (R100-R300, R500-R700, R900-R1100), 10000 samples per user; Section II models the channel as Saleh-Valenzuela (p. 2).
test_conditions: p. 4: 80% of the overall sample trains the model, same DeepMIMO regions throughout; NMSE swept over SNR; no new scenario, band, or array configuration is tested.
baselines: p. 4: Non-learned LS [20] and MMSE [5]; learned CL-based NN [9] and FL-based NN [11]; HNet and HReNet are compared with each other.
metrics: p. 4: NMSE in dB versus SNR (per region and whole cell); region-classification accuracy versus global rounds (Fig. 5); communication overhead of training.
complexity: p. 4: Parameter counts, PHNet = 2193536 versus PNN = 2171456 (1% more), and training communication overhead T_E = 6*PE*T*Kr; no FLOPs or runtime reported.
openness: none; only the public DeepMIMO dataset [21] is used (p. 4), and no code or data of its own is released
first_notes: Included, area 2: FL only trains the channel estimator, with model parameters sent to the BS and aggregated digitally (p. 3), so it is not area 7. q1 and q5 rest on the DeepMIMO O1 scenario named on p. 4; the paper does not explain how the RIS cascaded channel is derived from it. q3: the NN baselines are attributed to refs [9] and [11] but are described as a nine-convolution-layer single network (p. 4), which a reviewer could read as an ablation of the proposed method. q4: the parameter counts are used to compute the FL training overhead (p. 4), which alone would not count, but the counts themselves are reported, so q4 is marked 1; the reviewer may want to confirm. Training targets are called the LS-estimator output on p. 4, while the dataset pairs on p. 2 are (y, G).

title: DARENet: Data Arrangement Neural Network for Eigenvector-Based CSI Feedback

q2_support: p. 4: "superior performance across all the datasets examined" is reported dataset by dataset (Table II); no statement trains on one dataset and tests on another, and the train/test split is never described.
q3_support: p. 4: "in comparison with the state-of-the-art benchmark, EVCsiNet" and PolarDenseNet are both learned; the codebooks appear only on p. 1 ("conventional codebook methods"), so no non-learned baseline is compared.
q4_support: p. 4: "DARENet requires fewer Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) and has a smaller number of trainable parameters"; Table III gives 114.8682 M FLOPs and 0.3854 M parameters for DARENet (W=64, n=3).
q5_support: p. 1: "testing on 5 public datasets"; p. 3 footnote 1 gives the link "https://wirelessintelligence.com/#/dataSet?id=2c92185c7e3f1aa4017e3f2b9d6e0000" for datasets 1 to 5.
function: p. 1-3: CSI feedback: a CNN autoencoder compresses downlink CSI eigenvectors into Q feedback bits at the UE and recovers them at the BS.
system: p. 2: Downlink MIMO, BS with Ntx=32 cross-polarized antennas, UE with Nrx=4, single stream, 12-13 subbands; 3.5 or 4 GHz, 10 MHz bandwidth (Table I); no RIS.
method: p. 3-4: CNN encoder-decoder (data arrangement, IB-Blocks with instance/batch normalization and SE attention, uniform quantization); supervised against true eigenvectors with loss 1-SGCS; 50 epochs.
data_channel: p. 2-3: Five public datasets, channel models CDL-A, CDL-C, UMa LoS, CDL-A, UMi (Table I); 32x4 cross-polarized antennas; 3.5 or 4 GHz; UE speed 3-30 km/h.

title: Adversarial Attacks Against Double RIS-Assisted MIMO Systems-Based Autoencoder in Finite-Scattering Environments
function: p. 1: Adversarial attack (PGD-based perturbations) on an autoencoder-based double RIS-MIMO link; the autoencoder is the attacked system, and security is not one of the seven areas.
first_notes: Excluded on function. The paper studies adversarial attacks: p. 1: "This paper explores adversarial attacks against a double reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted multiple-input and multiple-output (MIMO)-based autoencoder". The proposed attack RMAEP is an iterative PGD algorithm with no trained parameters (Algorithm 1, p. 3), and the autoencoder (p. 2-3) is only the victim: p. 4: "we will study the effectiveness of adversarial attacks in damaging legitimate devices". Attack and security analysis is not one of the seven areas (it is akin to anti-jamming). no_learning could also be argued because the proposed method is an iterative algorithm; function was chosen because a learned transceiver (RIS phase prediction and decoder, p. 3) is present. The PDF is the arXiv preprint 2410.20103v1 (26 Oct 2024) and prints no DOI.
second_notes: The PDF is arXiv:2410.20103v1. Its title and four authors match the Crossref record of the DOI (IEEE Wireless Commun. Lett., 2025). Code no_learning: the method that the paper proposes and evaluates is a white-box adversarial attack. p. 4: "we propose Algorithm 1, named RIS-MIMO adversarial example-based PGD (RMAEP), to optimize the adversarial perturbation vector". Algorithm 1 (p. 3) runs projected gradient descent with a binary search on the perturbation vector and has no trained parameters, although p. 2 says the attack can "learn". The learned part is a 1D-CNN autoencoder whose CNNs set the phase shifts of the two RISs and decode the symbols (p. 2: "We employ one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to replace the physical components of these blocks"). It is only the system under attack (p. 2: "legitimate learning-based devices that can replace the RIS-aided MIMO system and suffer from attackers"). It is never compared with a detection or RIS baseline: all comparisons are between attacks, on the SER (p. 5: "RMAEF [8], the jamming attack [12], and the secured system (no attack) [7]"). For the reviewer: if RMAEP counts as learned, the code becomes function, because an adversarial attack is a security function (like anti-jamming) outside the seven areas. If the victim autoencoder counts as the method, the work would be included in area 1, since the main metric is the SER (Nt = Nr = 16, two RISs of 32 elements, p. 4).

title: Robust Learning-Based Data-Aided Channel Estimator in Time-Varying MIMO Channels
function: No learned component: the reinforcement learning policy reduces to the closed-form combining weight of Theorem 1 and eq. (23), computed from error variances without training (pp. 3-4).
first_notes: Excluded as no_learning. The letter calls its data-aided channel estimator reinforcement learning, but p. 3 says "the optimal policy is simplified from the following theorem" after fixing eta = 0 and the most likely transition, and Theorem 1 (eq. 22-23, p. 3-4) gives a closed-form weight alpha = e_mod / (e_data + e_mod) from error variances. Algorithm 1 (p. 4) is an online recursive update. The paper has no neural network, no training data, no training phase and no trained parameter; the offline process (p. 4) only estimates the initial error variance. If the reviewer reads the MDP and reinforcement learning framing as learning, the work would fall in area 2 (channel estimation, NMSE and FER).
second_notes: Title and DOI 10.1109/LWC.2025.3551140 are on p. 1, so the PDF matches. The paper frames its data-aided MIMO channel estimator as reinforcement learning, but nothing is learned from data or experience. p. 3: "the conventional data-driven approach [7] is not applicable to this MDP. To solve the MDP efficiently, a reinforcement learning algorithm in [10] is introduced by approximating the transition and value functions"; the approximations are the most likely transition under correct detection, eq. (21), and "setting η = 0" (p. 3). p. 4: Theorem 1 gives the policy in closed form, α_r(S) = ê_mod/(ê_data + ê_mod), eq. (23), and Algorithm 1 only does "Compute the optimal policy π⋆(S) from (23)" at each time slot. p. 5, Appendix B: "The optimal policy in (23) can be directly derived from (31), whose partial derivative satisfies zero." The only offline step estimates a statistic, not a model (p. 4: "The offline process is applied to estimate initial error variance"). The estimator is therefore a closed-form, decision-directed linear combination of a Gauss-Markov model-based estimate and a data-aided LMMSE estimate; learning appears only as framing and in the baseline RL-LMMSE [8] (p. 4). Borderline because the title says learning-based: if the reviewer counts this MDP solution as learned, it would be area 2 (channel estimation, NMSE and FER) with q1 0 (Rayleigh fading with first-order Gauss-Markov evolution, pp. 1-2), q2 0 (nothing trained; only zeta = 1e-3 and 1e-2), q3 1 (Conv. LMMSE and RL-LMMSE [8] on FER, p. 4), q4 1 (FLOPs and complexity order O(6Ntx^2 Nd + 19Ntx^3), pp. 4-5), q5 0 (no code or data released).

test_conditions: One street scene, 6000 training and 600 test samples; speed 10-100 km/h evaluated per speed (Fig. 4); SNR sweep, trained at 0-25 dB (Fig. 5) (pp. 4-5).
baselines: Learned: LSTM, Transformer [4], CNN; scheme without sensing assistance (communication CSI only, type not specified); ablations without channel attention, cross-attention, LLM; no classical predictor (pp. 4-5).

Historical CSI is assumed perfectly known (footnote 2, p. 3). The file is the arXiv preprint v1 of 14 May 2025 (arXiv:2505.09141v1); the DOI is not printed in the file.

title: Over-the-Air Inference Through Analog Computation Over Multi-Hop MIMO Networks
function: no_learning: relay precoders come from gradient descent on a convex problem (p. 4); the trained network is the image-classification application served by the link (p. 2).
first_notes: Exclusion no_learning (Step 1, item 3). The physical-layer design is classical optimization. p. 1: "the precoding matrix for each hop is obtained by the corresponding relay terminal by solving an optimization problem". p. 4: "It is easy to show that the optimization problem is convex, and can be solved via gradient descent". The only learned element is PrototypeNet, an image classifier trained offline on Fashion MNIST. p. 2: "We consider an image classification problem over a multihop MIMO network". It is not federated learning. p. 1: "we adopt offline centralized training to obtain the neural network weights". No learned precoder, detector or estimator appears. If the reviewer treats PrototypeNet as a learned part of the link, the code would be function instead, because over-the-air inference is none of the seven areas. The channel is i.i.d. CN(0,1) (p. 2) and the results are quantitative (p. 4-5).
second_notes: Page 1 holds the title of the DOI (Bian, Hua, Gunduz, 'Over-the-Air Inference Through Analog Computation Over Multi-Hop MIMO Networks', IEEE WCL 14(11), 2025). Reason no_learning. The physical-layer function is the precoder of each MIMO hop, and it is computed by a classical optimization: p. 1: "the precoding matrix for each hop is obtained by the corresponding relay terminal by solving an optimization problem, where the goal is to approximate the PrototypeNet weights with the effective channel matrix"; p. 4: "It is easy to show that the optimization problem is convex, and can be solved via gradient descent" (Algorithm 1). The learned element, PrototypeNet, is the image classifier (Fashion-MNIST, p. 4) whose inference the link computes over the air, so learning is the application that the link serves; the destination's learned FC layer outputs the image class (p. 2), it does not recover transmitted symbols. The federated-learning exception does not apply: p. 1: "we adopt offline centralized training to obtain the neural network weights", in contrast with training over the air. If the reviewer counts the channel-aware training of PrototypeNet (noise injection and power term in the loss, p. 3) as a learned physical-layer component, the next code that applies is function: over-the-air inference is not model aggregation across devices (area 7) and the precoders are not learned (area 3). Codes source_type, survey, system, and results do not apply: it is a research letter with simulation results (p. 4-5) and M = 49 antennas per node (p. 4).

title: UQML Based Precoder Optimization for RSMA-LEO Satellite Networks

system: LEO satellite BS, Nt = 12 antennas, N = 8 single-antenna ground stations (MISO, 1-layer RSMA), 28 GHz, Rician fading; no RIS (p. 2, 4-5).
method: Unsupervised quantum machine learning: parameterized quantum circuit, data re-uploading, L = 2, 512 shots, loss = negative sum rate, parameter-shift gradients, outputs mapped to WMMSE-style precoders (p. 3-4).
data_channel: Own LEO simulator: path loss, Rician fading, synthetic per-GS Doppler 100-1000 Hz; training and testing CSI generated independently, disjoint; no 3GPP model or measured data (p. 2, 4).
test_conditions: Disjoint training and testing CSI generated from the Doppler-variant LEO model; sum rate over 50 CSI realizations, SNR 0-20 dB, Nt = 12, N = 8 (p. 4-5).

The quantum circuit runs in IBM Qiskit, and p. 3: "with optimization currently performed on ground-based quantum processors". UCML counts as the learned baseline because it is a CNN adopted from DCLPNN [6]. title: Neural OTFS Receiver Without Training Requirements
q1_support: p. 4: "We use the 3GPP tapped delay line (TDL) channel model [21]"; results use TDL-B and TDL-E, and [21] is TR 38.901 (p. 5).
q2_support: p. 1: "requiring no datasets and training"; the proposed receiver has no training stage, so no trained model is tested on unseen conditions, and its NN is fitted again for every received signal. Only the trained BPICNet baselines are tested under mismatch (p. 5).
q3_support: p. 4: "The classical threshold based channel estimation [6]"; p. 4: "OTFS detector in [4] with the MMSE channel estimator as a representative for a trained DNN-based JCED"; NMSE and SER comparisons in Fig. 3 (p. 4-5).
q4_support: p. 5: "The comparison of the computational complexity is summarized in Table I, where the number of multiplications is used for evaluation."; Table I also lists run times.
q5_support: p. 1: "Data is available on-line at https://github.com/HaoChang1/UNN-JCED."
function: Joint channel estimation and symbol detection in the delay-Doppler domain for OTFS with superimposed pilots, using untrained neural networks optimized per received signal (p. 1-3).
system: SISO OTFS, 16x16 delay-Doppler grid, superimposed pilot, 4-QAM, fc = 6 GHz, up to 506 km/h, P = 8 reflectors; no RIS (p. 2, 4).
method: UNN-JCED: untrained fully connected CENN (channel) and SDNN (detection), unsupervised per-signal Adam fitting of received-signal reconstruction loss, BPIC refinement; no dataset, no offline training (p. 3-4).
data_channel: Simulated 3GPP TDL-B (NLoS) and TDL-E (LoS) channels per TR 38.901, delay spread 1/(M Δf); BPICNet baselines trained on them, the proposed method needs no dataset (p. 4-5).
test_conditions: Proposed: no training; tested on TDL-B and TDL-E, 168-506 km/h, P = 4-10. BPICNet baselines trained on one channel or P = 4, tested on mismatch (p. 4-5).
baselines: Non-learned: threshold estimation [6], MMSE, Threshold-MP [6], Threshold-EP and Ideal-EP [5]. Learned: BPICNet-JCED (BPICNet [4] with MMSE), Threshold/Ideal-UNN-BPIC [13] (p. 4).

openness: Footnote: "Data is available on-line at https://github.com/HaoChang1/UNN-JCED" (p. 1); contents not inspected.
first_notes: Borderline for Step 1 item 3: the proposed networks are untrained and their parameters are fitted per received signal with Adam on a loss (p. 3-4). I treat them as a learned component of the receiver, so the work is included in area 4. If the reviewer reads learned as trained on a dataset, the code would be no_learning. q1: the power delay profile follows TDL-B and TDL-E, while the delay-Doppler channel with P reflectors is the paper's own construction (p. 2, 4); marked met because the paper states the 3GPP TDL model, for the reviewer to confirm. q3: BPICNet-JCED is built by the authors from BPICNet [4] and MMSE, and [13] is their earlier UNN-BPIC. q5: the footnote says Data, and I did not open the repository.

title: DRL-Based Joint Beamforming and UAV Deployment Optimization for STAR-RIS-Assisted Over-the-Air Federated Learning
q1_support: p. 2: "modeled via their respective array responses" - the paper defines its own LoS ULA channel and sets path-loss parameters itself (p. 4); it names no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel.
q2_support: p. 5: "versus the total number of clients K" - only a sweep over K and the MSE requirement in one simulated setup; the paper never states a test on an unseen scenario, band or K, nor whether agents are retrained per K.

q4_support: p. 4: "lightweight and computationally efficient" - only a qualitative remark about DDQN; no complexity order, FLOPs, parameter count or runtime is reported for the method.
q5_support: p. 5: "We use a CNN model on the MNIST dataset" - MNIST is a public dataset of the learning task alone; the channel is a custom simulation (p. 2) and no code or data link or DOI is given.
function: SAC learns BS beamforming and STAR-RIS coefficients, DDQN learns UAV hovering position, to maximize clients admitted to over-the-air FL aggregation under an MSE limit (p. 1, 3).
system: BS with M=6 antennas, K single-antenna clients, UAV-mounted STAR-RIS with N=30 elements (energy splitting, coupled phase shifts), LoS ULAs; carrier frequency not stated (p. 2, 4).
method: Reinforcement learning: SAC (continuous beamforming and RIS actions) plus DDQN (discrete UAV positions) under one shared reward; FedAvg trains the CNN being aggregated (p. 2-4).
data_channel: Custom simulated LoS channel (ULA array responses, path-loss exponents 3 and 2.2); CNN on MNIST for the FL task; no standard or measured channel (p. 2, 4-5).
test_conditions: Training and test conditions not separated: one simulated setting (M=6, N=30, clients in two fixed regions); curves swept over MSE requirement kappa and total clients K (p. 4-5).
baselines: Ideal-AirFL (all clients, no error), IPS, CPS, CRIS, R-Phase (random STAR-RIS coefficients, SAC beamformer), random UAV position; no earlier published aggregation design or other learned method (p. 4-5).
metrics: Number of participating clients versus MSE requirement and versus K; FL prediction accuracy (CNN, MNIST) versus aggregation rounds and MSE requirement (p. 5).
complexity: none
first_notes: Area 7 over area 3: the problem solved is over-the-air aggregation itself, since beamforming, STAR-RIS and client count serve the aggregation MSE limit (p. 1-3). UAV placement is learned jointly with the physical-layer decision, so above_phy does not apply. Carrier frequency not stated.

title: GumbelRIS: End-to-End CNN-Based 2-Bit Phase Optimization for Large-Scale RIS-Aided MIMO Systems
q1_support: p. 2: "3GPP-compliant path loss and beamforming models" - the public SimRIS simulator (5G mmWave, indoor office, Table I) also gives the "3GPP-compliant UMi Outdoor Street Canyon" (p. 3); TR 38.901 is not named, flagged in notes.
q2_support: p. 3: "evaluated in both a 3GPP-compliant UMi Outdoor Street Canyon and a strict NLOS scenario" after training on the indoor office layout (p. 2); p. 2: "generalizes robustly without retraining". The training data of the outdoor and NLOS tests are not described.
q3_support: p. 3: "Metaheuristics - AGA [12], [13] and WaOA [14], deep learning algorithms - DRL [6] and GNN [8]" - all compared on capacity (Fig. 2, Table II, p. 4).
q4_support: p. 3: "approximately 28 million FLOPs per forward pass" and "35,552 trainable parameters"; inference latency is measured and plotted as execution time (p. 3, Fig. 2 on p. 4).
q5_support: p. 3: "The codes used in this letter are available on GitHub" - link in ref. [15] on p. 5: https://github.com/Kinza232/GumbleRIS.
function: CNN maps channel matrices (BS-RIS, RIS-UE, direct) to discrete 2-bit RIS phase shifts that maximize MIMO channel capacity (p. 1-3).
system: Reflecting RIS with 256 elements (sizes 4 to 256, 2-bit), 64-element planar BS array, 64-element planar UE array, direct plus RIS path, 28 GHz indoor office (p. 2).
method: End-to-end CNN (Conv2D, global pooling, dense head), trained unsupervised with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and a negative-capacity loss; hard arg-max at inference (p. 3).
data_channel: SimRIS (3D 5G mmWave, 3GPP-compliant path loss and beamforming), indoor office; 10,000 snapshots split 60/20/20; UMi street canyon and NLOS scenarios also tested (p. 2-3).

baselines: Non-learned: AGA (refs. 12-13) and WaOA (ref. 14) metaheuristics. Learned: DRL (ref. 6), GNN (ref. 8); MLP ablation (p. 3-4).
metrics: Mean achievable capacity (bps/Hz), execution/inference time, standard deviation and 95% confidence intervals over Monte Carlo runs, FLOPs and parameter count (p. 3-4).

openness: Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kinza232/GumbleRIS (p. 3, ref. 15 on p. 5); channel simulator SimRIS is public (p. 2).
first_notes: Area 3, RIS phase configuration. Please confirm q1: SimRIS is a public simulator that the paper calls 3GPP-compliant (path loss, beamforming, UMi street canyon) and 'a standard 5G channel model' (p. 2), but TR 38.901 is never cited by number. Please confirm q2: generalization without retraining is claimed (p. 1-2) and outdoor and NLOS scenarios are evaluated (p. 3), but the training protocol for those tests is not detailed.

title: Deep Learning-Based Composite Channel Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces-Aided Systems
q1_support: p. 4: "100 different Raleigh fading channel realizations" - the paper's own Rayleigh simulation; no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured channel is used.
q2_support: p. 5: "Both the training and testing are performed within the aforementioned SNR range" - held-out part of the same Rayleigh data; no other scenario, antenna count, RIS size, pilot count or band is tested.
q3_support: p. 5: "compared to LS and MMSE under varying SNR conditions" (Fig. 3) and "compared with several benchmark algorithms, including MLP, SRNet [6], SRDnNet [7], and JDCNet [8]" (Fig. 4), both on NMSE.
q4_support: p. 4: "Table I summarizes the computational complexities of the LS, LMMSE, and DL-Based channel estimation methods"; the proposed method has online complexity O(L1^2 + fCNN), about O(1x10^6) against O(1x10^11) for LS.

system: Uplink: M=30-antenna BS, K=6-antenna UE, passive reflecting RIS with N=30 elements, block flat fading, Tp=192 pilots; band not stated, footnote cites sub-6 GHz scattering (p. 2, 4).
method: Supervised CNN (three conv layers, two 1024-unit dense layers, 50% dropout); input stacks real, imaginary, magnitude of received subblocks; trained on labeled channel pairs with Adam (p. 3-4).

baselines: Non-learned: LS and LMMSE. Learned: MLP, SRNet (ref. 6), SRDnNet (ref. 7), JDCNet (ref. 8) (p. 5).
metrics: NMSE versus SNR (0 to 20 dB), with and without direct channel; analytical complexity orders; rate and pilot analyses mentioned but omitted (p. 4-5).

Footnote 2 on p. 2 justifies the unstructured channel model for rich-scattering sub-6 GHz systems but the simulated band is not stated. Results on rate versus SNR and pilots versus SNR are mentioned on p. 5 but omitted, so they are not counted for q2.

title: Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge-Based Channel Estimation for MIMO ISAC Systems
q1_support: p. 2: "we adopt a scattering channel model [1]" - own simulated ULA sensing channel with LoS UE channels; no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is used.
q2_support: p. 4: "A total of 10,000 Monte Carlo samples are generated (7,500 for training, 2,500 for testing)" - held-out split of the same data plus an SNR sweep; footnote 1 (p. 2) claims good results with non-orthogonal pilots but reports none.
q3_support: p. 4: "we compare the proposed method with previous channel estimation algorithms, including LMMSE, DnCNN, Double-CNN [3], pix2pix GAN [4], and the Brownian bridge [11]" - NMSE versus SNR in Fig. 2 (LS also plotted).
q4_support: p. 4: "the overall complexity for inference is" O(N^3 + S N^2), with S = 1 step, against O(N^6) for LMMSE (Section IV-B).
q5_support: p. 4: "A total of 10,000 Monte Carlo samples are generated" - self-generated simulation data; no code or data link or DOI appears in the letter.
function: Diffusion Schrödinger-bridge model refines the least-squares estimate of the ISAC sensing (target-echo) channel into the ground-truth channel, in one inference step (p. 1-4).
system: MIMO ISAC: transmitting and receiving BS with N=32-antenna ULAs, K UEs (LoS), L=3 targets, orthogonal pilots tau_p=N+K; carrier band not stated (p. 2, 4).
method: Generative: diffusion Schrödinger bridge (VE-DSB) with time-conditioned UNet (ResBlocks, self-attention), data-prediction loss on paired LS and true channels, supervised, ODE sampling with S=1 (p. 3-4).
data_channel: Own simulation: scattering sensing channel (L=3 targets, ULA steering vectors), LoS UE channels; 10,000 samples split 7,500 training and 2,500 testing; no standard channel (p. 2, 4).
test_conditions: Same simulated setup for training and testing (N=32, L=3, 7,500/2,500 split); NMSE evaluated for SNR from -10 to 10 dB; no unseen scenario (p. 4).
baselines: Non-learned: LS, LMMSE. Learned: DnCNN, Double-CNN (ref. 3), UNet, pix2pix GAN (ref. 4), Brownian bridge diffusion (ref. 11) (p. 4-5).
metrics: NMSE in dB versus SNR; number of inference steps; heatmap examples; effect of training timesteps on NMSE (p. 4-5).
complexity: Inference O(N^3 + S N^2) with S=1 inference step (LS O(N^3), network O(N^2) FLOPs), against LMMSE O(N^6) and S>=100 of earlier diffusion works (p. 4).
first_notes: Area 2: the learned method estimates the sensing (target-echo) channel of an ISAC system that also serves K communicating UEs (p. 2), so it is not excluded as sensing alone. K and the carrier frequency are not given in the simulation setup (p. 4). The claim of adaptation to complex channel models (p. 5) and the non-orthogonal pilot claim (p. 2) have no reported test.

title: DRL-Based User Fairness in Beyond Diagonal Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface-Assisted Extremely Large Antenna Array Systems
q1_support: p. 2: "The near field channel model is formulated in (1) shown at the bottom of the next page based on [11]"; custom LoS near-field and far-field models, no 3GPP TR 38.901, DeepMIMO or measured data is used.
q2_support: p. 5: "The impacts of the number of antennas Nt and the number of BDRIS elements M are also analyzed"; these are sweeps, network sizes depend on Nt and M (p. 4), and no test of one trained model on an unseen scenario is stated.
q3_support: p. 4: "is compared with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)" and SAC; p. 4: "an ELAA setup with random transmit beamforming vectors" as the non-learned baseline; compared on rates in Figs. 4, 5, 8.
q4_support: p. 4: "the total asymptotic complexity of the algorithm can be shown derived as" O(M^3 + (K Nt + M^2 + K) n1 + n1 n2 + (K Nt + M^2) n2).
q5_support: p. 4: "The experiment is repeated over 10 random seeds with hyperparameters in Table I"; own simulator, no code or data link or DOI, no public channel dataset.
function: Joint design of BS transmit beamformers and BDRIS reconfiguration matrix to maximize the minimum user rate (user fairness) with a learned policy (p. 1-3).
system: Multi-user downlink, BS ULA with Nt=50 antennas, fully connected beyond-diagonal reflecting RIS (BDRIS) with M=36 elements, near-field BS links, far-field BDRIS-user links, 2.4 GHz (p. 2, 4).
method: PPO actor-critic deep reinforcement learning, hidden layers of 128 and 64 neurons; reward is the minimum user rate; QR projection enforces the unitary BDRIS constraint (p. 3-4).
data_channel: Own simulated LoS channels: near-field spherical-wave BS-user and BS-BDRIS (model of Bjornson and Sanguinetti), far-field BDRIS-user with path loss; no dataset or measurements (p. 2).
test_conditions: Same simulated setup for training and testing; users random in a 150 m x 150 m grid, 10 seeds; perfect/imperfect CSI; Nt and M varied (p. 4-5).
baselines: Learned: DDPG, SAC, RIS-ELAA DRL scheme of [16], ELAA-only DRL without RIS. Non-learned: ELAA with random transmit beamforming (p. 4).
metrics: Reward (minimum user rate), mean rate, outage probability from CDF of user rates, sum-rate, max-min rate, convergence episodes (p. 4-5).
complexity: Big-O order O((KNt+M^2)(n1+n2)+n1(n2+K)+M^3) from forward/backward passes plus QR; stated lower than the method of [8]; no runtime or FLOPs (p. 4).
first_notes: Area 3: the learned PPO policy outputs both the BS beamformers and the BDRIS matrix (p. 3). The Fig. 5 legend (p. 5) lists Proposed, ELAA only, RIS ELAA [16], Random, and Fig. 8 shows Proposed, RIS NF, NF Only, Random. The complexity of [8] is compared only analytically (p. 4).

title: Deep Learning Prediction of Beam Coherence Time for Near-Field TeraHertz Networks
q1_support: p. 4: "close-in (CI) model in [13, eq. (1)] with a path loss exponent of" - only the path gains follow a measurement-based sub-THz path loss model; the spherical-wave multipath channel with 2 random scatterers and the Gauss-Markov trajectories are a custom simulation (pp. 2-3), with no standardized model or measured data.
q2_support: p. 5: "model is trained only for 142 and 280 GHz" - the effective rate in Fig. 5 is also evaluated at 180 and 220 GHz, carrier frequencies absent from the training set.
q3_support: p. 4: "closely to the ideal upper-bound, we omit other baselines and" - only non-learned references are compared (numerical T_B search, statistical T_C, ideal upper bound); no earlier learned method or standard network is included as a baseline.
q4_support: p. 3: "the measured average inference time per sample is" - 5.3 microseconds per sample for the proposed FNN, against about 2 seconds for the numerical T_B search with N = 512.
q5_support: p. 1: "relies on relevant simulated data" - the 2.5 x 10^5-sample dataset is built by the authors from their own simulation (p. 3); no code or data link or DOI is given, and no public or measured dataset is used.
function: Predicts beam coherence time T_B (time until beam gain falls below a threshold) so the AP updates its near-field beam only when needed, reducing overhead (p. 3).
system: THz hybrid near/far-field link: AP with 512-element ULA, single-antenna mobile UE, 142 GHz (and 280 GHz), 20 MHz; L = 2 scatterers; no RIS (pp. 2-3).
method: Feedforward network (6 fully connected layers, 12-dimensional input), supervised offline training with smooth L1 loss on labels from the numerical solver (p. 3).
data_channel: Own simulation: Gauss-Markov trajectories, spherical-wave channel with close-in path loss [13], 2.5 x 10^5 samples split 80/10/10; labels from numerical solution of (7) (pp. 3-4).
test_conditions: Trained at 142 and 280 GHz on three mobility types; tested on held-out 10% and, in Fig. 5, also at 180 and 220 GHz (pp. 3, 5).
baselines: Numerical T_B (exhaustive search, ground truth), statistical T_C updates every channel coherence time, ideal upper bound with perfect CSI and no overhead; no learned baseline (p. 4).
metrics: Effective rate in bps/Hz including beam-update overhead, average beam-update duration, inference time (pp. 3-5).
complexity: Measured average inference time 5.3 microseconds per sample versus about 2 seconds for the numerical approach with N = 512 at 142 GHz (p. 3).
first_notes: Area 3 is borderline: the network outputs the beam coherence time, that is, how long a beam stays valid, while the beam vector itself is computed from the UE position (p. 4). I treat beam-update control as beam management (area 3), not channel prediction (area 2) or link adaptation; the reviewer should confirm. q1 is 0: the close-in sub-THz path-loss model of [13] sits inside a custom simulator and the data are simulated, not measured. q2 is 1 from the training statement on p. 3 and p. 5 and the markers of Fig. 5, which I read from the page image (points at 142, 180, 220, 280 GHz). q3 is 0: no learned baseline; RNN and LSTM are only mentioned as not used (p. 3). The transformer-based CSIformer classifies the number of targets and their section from CSI estimated at the communication receiver (p. 6): opportunistic sensing and localization, an excluded function. Area 5 does not apply: with communication-centric signals "it is not possible to optimize or adapt the waveform design, beamforming, or power allocation" (p. 2). The paper calls itself an ISAC framework (p. 3), which the reviewer may weigh. If overturned: code link on p. 1, QuaDRiGa and NIST Q-D ray tracing on p. 7.

Earlier checks pass: a research article that proposes and evaluates a learned (transformer) method on CSI, not above the physical layer. The PDF matches the DOI (title and DOI on p. 1).
