title: Analysis With Deep Learning of Robust UAV-Mounted Active IRS NOMA Networks With Imperfections
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
function: No learned physical-layer function: the DNN only predicts outage probability and ergodic capacity (pp. 10-11); phase shifts, power and UAV position use closed-form or search methods (pp. 4, 8-9).
first_notes: Title on page 1 matches the DOI. Analytical outage and capacity study of a UAV-mounted active IRS NOMA network. The DNN (80,485 parameters, p. 12) is a supervised regression surrogate with 14 inputs and five outputs (outage probabilities and ergodic capacities), trained on Monte-Carlo data (pp. 10-11). Phase shifts are set coherently in closed form (p. 18); power allocation and UAV position come from Algorithms 1 and 2 (pp. 8-9). Code function would also apply, since performance prediction is none of the seven areas.
second_notes: Title and DOI match on p. 1. Reason no_learning. The work is a performance analysis (closed-form outage probability, ergodic capacity and throughput over Nakagami-m fading) of a UAV-mounted active/passive IRS NOMA network in which, p. 4: "both the base station and users utilize single-antenna devices". Its only learned component is a supervised multi-output DNN that maps 14 system parameters to OP and ergodic capacity, p. 10: "This section introduces a DNN framework designed to efficiently estimate OP and ergodic capacity", "offering a practical alternative to the demanding nature of mathematical analysis"; p. 4: "we develop a DNN model that offers a high-accuracy, low-latency data-driven alternative for OP and ergodic capacity prediction". No physical-layer decision is learned. The IRS phases are a closed-form coherent alignment, p. 4: "By employing a coherent phase shifting strategy, we derive the optimal signal-to-interference-plus-distortion-plus-noise ratio", and p. 18: "With perfect channel state information, we set the n-th element’s phase shift to" the closed-form value "for optimal channel gain". The NOMA power allocation is a line search, p. 8: "we introduce a straightforward search method to accurately determine the optimal" delta_1 (Algorithm 1). The UAV 3D position, which is above the physical layer anyway, uses p. 8: "an Alternating Optimization (AO) strategy is used" (Algorithm 2). The random-search hyperparameter tuning (p. 11) concerns only the predictor. If the reviewer counts the DNN metric predictor as a learned method, the next code that applies is function, since predicting OP and capacity solves none of the seven areas. The system code would not apply because the link has an IRS.

title: Signal Detection in Intelligent Reflecting Surface-Assisted NOMA Network Using LSTM Model: A ML Approach
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society

title: Toward Proactive, Secure and Efficient Space-Air-Ground Communications: Generative AI-Based DRL Framework
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
q1_support: p. 4: "adopt Nakagami-m fading for a more accurate representation"; the channel is a custom model with Rician factor, Doppler, delay and atmospheric loss (Table 2, page 11). No 3GPP TR 38.811 or 38.901, DeepMIMO or measured data is mentioned.
q2_support: p. 11: "was subjected to an extensive training duration of 2000" epochs for each experimental setup. The sweeps over HAP power, rate threshold, number of HAPs, users per HAP and altitude never say a model trained in one setting was tested in another.
q3_support: p. 10: "Optimal solution: in which we design an exhaustive" search (non-learned), plus the learned LSTM-DDQN [31] and DDQN [38]; all are compared on secrecy energy efficiency in Figs. 5-9 (pages 12-13).
q4_support: p. 9: "computational complexity per iteration can be expressed as:" followed on page 10 by O(KH + M^3 + HT + bm|theta|) per iteration and the total over I iterations and L agents (Eqs. 25-26).
q5_support: p. 10: "The simulations were implemented using Python 3.8.5 and" PyTorch 2.0 on the authors' own machine; the paper gives no link to code or data and uses no public dataset.
function: Gen-DRL (GAN actor, FC critic) jointly learns HAP trajectory, user-HAP association, beamforming and channel prediction to maximize secrecy energy efficiency in a LEO-HAP downlink (pp. 6-8).
system: LEO satellite UPA (Table 2 lists 265 antennas), three 64-antenna HAP UPAs, 21 users and 21 eavesdroppers with 16-antenna ULAs, 28 GHz, no RIS (pp. 4, 11).
method: Actor-critic deep reinforcement learning: GAN generator with Bi-LSTM as actor, fully connected critic, prioritized experience replay, Adam; 2000 training epochs per setup (pp. 7-9, 11).
data_channel: Custom simulated LEO and HAP channels (Nakagami-m stated, Rician factor 10 dB, 5 paths, Doppler, delay, atmospheric loss); users and eavesdroppers uniformly placed; no 3GPP model (pp. 4-5, 11).
test_conditions: Each experimental setup trained for 2000 epochs; sweeps of HAP power, rate threshold, number of HAPs, users per HAP, altitude; no train-then-test in unseen conditions (pp. 11-13).
baselines: Learned: LSTM-DDQN [31] and DDQN [38]; non-learned: exhaustive-search optimal solution as upper bound; no other classical heuristic (pp. 10, 12-13).
metrics: Secrecy energy efficiency versus HAP power, rate threshold, number of HAPs, users per HAP and altitude; reward convergence; gap to optimal, 5.1% for Gen-DRL (pp. 11-13).
complexity: Complexity per iteration O(KH + M^3 + HT + bm|theta|), total over I iterations and L agents; contrasted with LSTM-DDQN, DDQN, genetic search, exhaustive search; no runtime (pp. 9-10).
openness: none: no code or data link; simulations in Python 3.8.5 and PyTorch 2.0 on the authors' own machine (pp. 10-11).
first_notes: Included, area 6: Gen-DRL outputs beamforming (physical layer) jointly with HAP trajectory and user association (above the physical layer) and channel prediction. Under the satellite and aerial rule this passes above_phy, and NTN is more specific than areas 2 and 3. The system has no RIS (Fig. 1, page 4); Algorithm 2 on page 9 lists RIS among its inputs and some references are RIS-aided, but the model has none. The non-learned baseline is the exhaustive-search optimum. Complexity is asymptotic only, with no runtime.

title: Deep Compressed Sensing for Terahertz Ultra-Massive MIMO Channel Estimation
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
q1_support: p. 9: "channel simulator built on the measurement data in [55], [56]"; the authors adopt TeraMIMO, a published statistical THz simulator (ref. [8]) built on measurements, with their own near-field and rotation changes. It is not a 3GPP model, so see notes.

q4_support: p. 12: "We summarize the computation complexity of the aforementioned CE algorithms in Table 6"; page 13 gives DCS O(T Ns Np Nt Nr) against GAN O(R T' Ns Np Nt Nr), LS and LMMSE O(Nt^3 Nr^3), OMP O(S Nt Nr).
q5_support: p. 1: "Data is available on-line at https://github.com/ganghui0/dcs-thz-mimo-ce"; the repository link is stated on the first page. I did not open the link.
function: Channel estimation for wideband THz UM-MIMO: generative-network deep compressed sensing (DCS) recovers the channel from Np pilots via latent optimization with a few gradient steps (pp. 3, 6-8).
system: Multi-carrier THz UM-MIMO, 256 Tx and 32 Rx antennas (array-of-subarrays, hybrid beamforming), 300 GHz, 10 GHz bandwidth, 8 subcarriers, near field at 1 m; no RIS (pp. 4, 9).
method: DCGAN generator with latent-space gradient descent; offline training on ground-truth channels with NMSE plus RIP loss in a dual loop, meta-learning principle, no discriminator (pp. 3, 7-8).
data_channel: TeraMIMO statistical THz simulator built on measurement data, modified (AE-level spherical wave, receiver rotation, HITRAN absorption); 5000 training and 1000 test channels (p. 9, Table 2).
test_conditions: Trained on 5000 channels (LoS+NLoS, spacing lambda/2, rotation pi/6, 100 pilots); tested on 1000 channels and out-of-distribution pilots 10-200, LoS-only, spacing lambda/5, lambda/10, rotation 2pi/9 (pp. 9, 14).
baselines: Classical: LS, LMMSE, OMP; learned: pre-trained GAN estimator [23], [24] with the same generator, 10 restarts of 50 steps (pp. 12-13).
metrics: NMSE versus SNR (-20 to 15 dB), pilot length, latent dimension and optimization steps; training convergence in epochs; inference steps (pp. 10-14).
complexity: Table 6: DCS O(TNsNpNtNr), GAN O(RT'NsNpNtNr), LS and LMMSE O(Nt^3Nr^3), OMP O(SNtNr); 20 steps versus GAN's 500 (pp. 12-13).
first_notes: Included, area 2: DCS is a learned generative channel estimator for THz UM-MIMO. q1 is a proposal for the reviewer to confirm: the data come from TeraMIMO [8], a published statistical THz simulator built on measurement data [55], [56], modified by the authors (AE-level spherical wave, receiver rotation, HITRAN absorption, Poisson clusters and rays); it is neither a listed 3GPP model nor DeepMIMO (page 9). q3: the GAN baseline uses the same DCGAN generator as DCS but is an earlier published estimator [23], [24], so I counted it as a learned baseline and not as a variant of the proposed method.

title: Resource Allocation in STAR-RIS-Aided SWIPT With RSMA via Meta-Learning
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society

title: Data-Driven Beam-to-Gateway Matching and Adaptive Load Balancing for Multi-Beam GEO Satellite Systems
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
function: Above the physical layer: LSTM traffic and rain-attenuation forecasts feed gateway load balancing and beam-to-gateway matching, solved by non-learned optimization and genetic algorithm (p. 1-2, 11).
first_notes: Exclude, above_phy. Page 1 holds the title Data-Driven Beam-to-Gateway Matching and Adaptive Load Balancing for Multi-Beam GEO Satellite Systems, matching the DOI. It is a research article with simulation results (p. 13-15), so codes 1, 2 and 7 do not apply. The only learned element is a stacked multi-horizon LSTM that forecasts per-beam traffic demand and per-gateway rain attenuation (p. 2: "These forecasts are then used as inputs to an adaptive genetic algorithm that performs proactive, capacity-aware B2G matching and load balancing"); it takes no beam, power or resource decision. Capacity allocation and beam-to-gateway matching come from a convex problem and from AGA, GA, ACO and WLB heuristics, none learned (p. 8-11), for load balancing under QoE and blocking-probability targets: traffic steering and network management above the physical layer, with traffic prediction as the learned task. A reviewer who reads the matching as a non-learned physical-layer function could use no_learning instead.
second_notes: Title and DOI on p. 1 match the DOI given (published OJCOMS version). Exclusion no_learning: the physical-layer function of the work, feeder-link capacity allocation and beam-to-gateway matching of a multi-beam GEO satellite (satellite resource control), is solved by a closed form (p. 8, Proposition 1) and an adaptive genetic algorithm (p. 10-11), and is compared only with WLB, GA, ACO and branch and bound (p. 13-14); none of these is a trained model. Learning appears only as two LSTM forecasters whose outputs feed the optimizer (p. 2: "These forecasts are then used as inputs to an adaptive genetic algorithm"): per-beam traffic demand (traffic prediction, above the PHY) and per-gateway rain attenuation computed from Meteostat rain rates with ITU-R P.838-3 (p. 6-7). The authors set learned control aside (p. 2: RL approaches "suffer from the exponential growth of state and action spaces"). Alternative readings for the reviewer: if the LSTM forecasting is taken as the learned function, traffic forecasting is above the PHY (above_phy), while the rain LSTM forecasts the feeder-link SNR (p. 12, Figs. 10-11), which could be read as NTN channel prediction (area 2); the forecasters are evaluated only by training and test MSE curves, with no predictor baseline (p. 12).

(p. 7). The learned task is gesture recognition (p. 1: "we propose mmGAN, a semi-supervised method for ISAC-based gesture recognition"), a sensing inference like the excluded positioning or activity tasks, not the ISAC problem of area 5 (beams, waveforms, and resources that serve sensing and communication) nor any other area. The first page holds the title "mmGAN: Semi-Supervised GAN for Improved Gesture Recognition in mmWave ISAC Systems" and DOI 10.1109/OJCOMS.2025.3649235, so the PDF matches its DOI.

title: Integrated Sensing and Communication for Blockage Detection in V2X Networks
journal: IEEE Open Journal of the Communications Society
function: Detection and prediction of LiDAR and RF-power blockages and anomalies with an unsupervised Bayesian network (IC-GDBN); not beam, waveform or resource design, so none of the seven areas (p. 3: "predict and detect both sensor and power blockages").
first_notes: Excluded for function (Step 1, code 5). The learned component (growing neural gas clustering and the IC-GDBN dictionary, unsupervised) is learned, and it does not act above the physical layer, but its task is blockage detection and anomaly detection from 3D LiDAR tracks and received RF power (p. 1 abstract: "predict various types of LiDAR and RF power blockages"; p. 3: "Instead of designing physical communication systems"). second_notes: Reason function, shown on p. 3: "Instead of designing physical communication systems, a data-driven method ... (IC-GDBN), is introduced to predict and detect both sensor and power blockages within the ISAC framework." The RF branch is a scalar received-power trace computed from LiDAR/GPS positions with free-space path loss and Rician or Rayleigh fading (p. 7, Eq. (1); p. 12: "computation of received power signals using equation (1)"), so the method neither estimates nor predicts CSI, designs no beams or RIS, and allocates no ISAC beams, waveforms, or resources. For the reviewer: if RF-power blockage prediction were read as channel prediction (area 2), the work would still fail the system check, since the link is a 2.4 GHz single-antenna model with scalar gains Gtx = Grx = 10 dBi (Table 1, p. 15, read from the page image) and XBee 3 Zigbee modules in the campus setup (p. 5), with no RIS. title: MAGIC: Matching Game-Based Resource Allocation With Incomplete Information in Space Communication Network

The allocation is made by a non-learned three-sided matching game of users, access satellites and destination nodes under capacity limits (p. 6, p. 8, p. 9, p. 10; UoRA and SoRA, Algorithms 1 and 2). The objective is the sum of priorities of accessed users (p. 5). No transmit power, bandwidth, beam or channel value is learned (power is a given parameter, p. 3, p. 4), so the satellite exception of step 1.4 for learned power, resource or beam control does not apply: the problem is user association and access control. The paper says the RL helps 'predict and approach the complete network channel state information' (p. 5, p. 7), but its output is the binary preference flag rewarded by the completeness of the preference list (Eq. 29, p. 7), and no channel-prediction error is reported; results are matched users, AS revenue, user satisfaction, iterations and time versus greedy and random matching (p. 10-12). second_notes: Title and DOI 10.1109/TCOMM.2024.3368327 are on p. 1, so the PDF matches. Reviewer to confirm above_phy against an area 6 reading.

title: Dependency-Elimination MADRL: Scalable On-Board Resource Allocation for Feeder- and User-Link Integrated Satellite Communications

function: Learned beam hopping pattern and downlink power allocation per beam for a multi-beam LEO satellite with integrated feeder- and user-links (MADDPG); bandwidth allocation is non-learned (pp. 6-8).
system: LEO satellite relay (540 km), 20x25 UPA, 8 uplink/8 downlink beams, 49 cells, one GS, 19/29 GHz uplink/downlink, shadowed-Rician fading; no RIS (pp. 3, 11-12).
method: Multi-agent DDPG (DE-MADDPG), one actor-critic agent per beam, epsilon-greedy beam selection, state/reward decomposition, non-cooperation penalty; reinforcement learning, offline training (pp. 8-11).
data_channel: Own Python simulator: free-space path loss, shadowed-Rician fading (Omega 0.835, b0 0.126, m 10.01), ITU-R S.1528 beam pattern, Poisson traffic; parameters from Starlink and 3GPP [48] (pp. 3, 12).

baselines: Non-learned: Random and Greedy beam hopping with equal bandwidth and power. Learned: DeepBeam [8] (beam hopping only, average power) and CoMADRL [16] (common-reward MADRL) (p. 12).
metrics: System throughput (Gbps), service fairness (RCSR gap), constraint satisfaction rate, convergence curves versus episode (pp. 5, 12-13).

VI-B3 claims generalization over traffic distributions (Table V) without stating a train/test mismatch; reviewer to confirm. q3: CoMADRL [16] and DeepBeam [8] are cited earlier works but are described relative to the proposed method (common reward, average power), so check that they are not ablations.

function: Position-based downlink precoder generation: NN maps UE position and uplink reference CFRs of fixed wireless nodes (environment sensing) to the per-subcarrier precoder, without CSI feedback (pp. 4-5).

metrics: Spectral efficiency (bits/s/Hz) versus transmit power, feedback bits, number of FWNs and training time points; performance loss relative to perfect CSI for LoS and NLoS (pp. 10-11).
complexity: none; only the qualitative claim "low-complexity" (p. 2).
openness: none released; uses the public DeepMIMO generator (p. 8).

The high-level Pointer-TP agent assigns each UAV to an SN cluster, i.e. UAV trajectory planning (p. 9: the output is the index of the cluster assigned to each UAV; p. 1: it 'assigns each UAV to an appropriate cluster'). The low-level RA agent picks the SN that each UAV serves at each TDMA time step, i.e. user association or scheduling (p. 11: 'The RA agent determines the association between the UAV and the SNs in the assigned cluster at each time step'; p. 4: TDMA protocol). The transmit power is a constant (p. 5: 'the transmission power is a constant'), and no beam, bandwidth or power is learned (Table I, p. 12). Borderline point for the reviewer: the paper names the second agent 'resource allocation', and the aerial-link clause treats learned resource allocation as physical layer, but here the only 'resource' allocated is the choice of SN per time step, which is scheduling. If the reviewer reads it as physical-layer resource allocation, the work would be area 6 (single-antenna Rician A2G links, p. 4; quantitative simulation results, Figs. 8-16).
second_notes: Title on p. 1 matches the DOI. Passes source_type, survey and no_learning (pointer-network and actor-critic agents trained by RL). Fails above_phy. p. 2: "perform resource allocation at a small timescale by controlling the association between UAVs and SNs". p. 8: Pointer-TP "outputs the index of the cluster assigned to each UAV per time slot k". p. 11: "The RA agent determines the association between the UAV and the SNs in the assigned cluster at each time step" (one-hot SN choice). These are UAV trajectory/placement and user association/scheduling. The paper calls the second decision resource allocation (time per SN is the sum of association indicators, eq. (10), p. 5), but no physical-layer quantity is learned: SN power P_m is a given parameter (p. 4), p. 5: "the transmission power is a constant denoted as Pc", and the bandwidth is fixed at 1 MHz (Table I, p. 12). So the aerial-link exception for learned power, resource allocation, or beams does not apply. title: Attention-Based SIC Ordering and Power Allocation for Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access Networks
function: Learned actor picks the SIC decoding order and convex optimization sets power: NOMA resource allocation for weighted proportional fairness, none of the seven areas (pp. 1, 5).
first_notes: Excluded for function (Step 1, rule 5). arXiv v1 preprint, 20 pages read in full. The attention actor, trained with REINFORCE and a baseline network (p. 5), only generates the SIC decoding order; user powers come from a convex program (p. 7). The objective is weighted proportional fairness of rates (p. 1) and the paper lists its topic as resource allocation (p. 1, Index Terms), so no symbols are recovered and it is not area 1. Borderline for the reviewer: SIC ordering is a detection-order decision. The main model has single-antenna users and a scalar channel gain per user (pp. 3-4); a 2-antenna BS with MMSE equalization appears only as an extension (pp. 9, 15). A code link exists (pp. 1, 11), but items and criteria are left empty for an excluded work.
second_notes: Exclude, code function (first code that applies). The learned part is an attention-based actor network trained with REINFORCE with baseline. It maps user weights, maximum powers and channel gains to the SIC decoding order, and the power is then allocated by convex optimization (p. 5: 'X = {(wi, Pimax, gi)}i∈N, is fed into the actor network to generate the SIC ordering π'; 'we solve the subproblem P1 for the optimal power allocation p through convex optimization'; p. 7: 'interior-point method [56] of the CVX solver'). The objective and the metric are the network utility, a weighted sum of log Shannon rates (p. 4, problem P0; p. 11, Sec. 6.2 'Network Utility Performance'), and the index terms list 'resource allocation' (p. 1). This is NOMA resource allocation: the network does not take the received signal or recover symbols (area 1), estimate channels (area 2), or design precoders, beams or RIS (area 3), and the links are terrestrial, with no OTFS, ISAC, NTN or over-the-air FL. Codes 1 to 4 checked: a research article; a learned component makes a physical-layer decision; the SIC decoding order is a receiver decision, not in the above-PHY list. For the reviewer: area 1 could be weighed because SIC is multi-user detection and Sec. 5.1 adds a 2-antenna BS with MMSE equalization ('to detect symbols', p. 15). But the learned network only orders decoding for the rate utility, and no detection metric is reported. The main system has single-antenna users (p. 3) and a single-antenna BS ('Different from the single antenna scenario', p. 9). Identity: the PDF is arXiv:2407.14740v1 (p. 1), and Crossref lists the same title and authors for this DOI (IEEE Trans. Mobile Comput., Feb. 2025).

title: Dual Network Computation Offloading Based on DRL for Satellite-Terrestrial Integrated Networks
function: Excluded (above_phy): the DRL learns the computation-offloading location (satellite or cloud) of IoT tasks, an edge-computing decision above the physical layer (pp. 1, 5, 8).
first_notes: Exclusion above_phy. The learned element is a DNN that outputs the binary offloading-location vector for 10 IoT devices (p. 5: "xn = 0 indicates that the task is computed locally on the satellite, and xn = 1 indicates that the task is computed at the cloud service center"; p. 8: "produces an output in the form of a floating-point N-dimensional vector"; Table III on p. 11 lists 10 output nodes). The abstract on p. 1 calls it a "deep reinforcement learning-based computation offloading decision algorithm". The only radio resource in the problem, the channel bandwidth, is not learned: p. 8: "DRLO employs channel bandwidth allocation algorithm based on the Lagrange multiplier method"; p. 10: "We employ a binary search method to solve for the Lagrange multiplier v". Although p. 7 writes the MDP action as (x_t, tau_t), the network output and the stored training labels are only the offloading vector (p. 8: "DRLO stores the inputs and decision as a triplet"), so no physical-layer decision is learned jointly with the offloading one. No physical-layer function (detection, channel estimation or feedback, precoding or beams, RIS, OTFS, ISAC, NTN power or beam control, over-the-air aggregation) is learned. Results (pp. 11-13) are a normalized cost ratio and run time, with a free-space path loss plus Rician fading channel (p. 11).
second_notes: Exclude, above_phy (p. 8). The learning acts on task offloading / edge computing decisions. p. 1: "we present a deep reinforcement learning-based computation offloading decision algorithm". p. 8: "The DNN takes the satellite network channel gain ht and computation workload Z t as inputs" and its output is quantized into "K candidate binary computation offloading location decision vectors"; then "DRLO employs channel bandwidth allocation algorithm based on the Lagrange multiplier method to generate τ" (Algorithm 2, binary search, p. 10). So the only learned decision is the offloading location (satellite vs cloud); the bandwidth allocation, the only resource decision on the satellite link, is classical, so no physical-layer decision is learned jointly with the offloading. no_learning was not used because the method itself is learned (DRL); above_phy names task offloading explicitly. Title and DOI on p. 1 match the record.

ReDBeam is a parallel optimization algorithm, p. 6: "it generates a sufficiently large number (denoted as L) of initial solutions within a promising search space ... we employ a scaling-based local search". Its 'data-driven' label means an empirical Wasserstein ambiguity set built from N noisy CSI samples (p. 5), and pp. 1-2 contrast the approach with learning: "unlike learning-based solutions, D2BF only requires limited CSI data samples collected in real-time and does not need a complicated offline training process". second_notes: Reason function, p. 5. The title on p. 1 matches the DOI. The learned method proposed is X-ZeroSec, an adversarial-input detector built from tree-based classifiers (a direct detector, a second detector trained on TreeSHAP attributions, and a stacking meta-model): p. 5: "detection methodology to filter out adversarial data"; p. 6: "employs a light ML model to classify received signals as either benign or adversarial". The DL beam predictor (six fully connected layers, DeepMIMO O1 and CM6) is the attacked model reproduced from Alkhateeb et al. [35], p. 7: "closely follows the methodology outlined by Alkhateeb et al. [35]", so learned beamforming appears only as the application being protected. The main metrics are detection metrics, p. 9: "main performance metrics: detection accuracy on previously encountered (seen) attacks", with achievable rate shown only as the effect of the filter (Figs. 6, 14, 17, 20). Detecting adversarial perturbations of received pilots is a physical-layer security task, like physical-layer authentication, and is not one of the seven areas. above_phy was considered and not applied: the detector classifies physical-layer received pilot signals (pp. 4-6), although it runs as an xApp, p. 17: "operating within the Near-Real-Time RIC". If the reviewer counted the reproduced beam predictor as the learned method, the work would fall in area 3.

second_notes: The title on p. 1 matches the DOI. Exclusion code above_phy. The learned method is a TD3-style DRL agent (double critics, delayed actor update, target networks). Its actions are 'uplink bandwidth aui(t), MEC server computing resource aci(t), and downlink bandwidth adi(t)' (p. 5) for the tasks in the execution queue. The goal is to 'improve the completion rate of collaborative sensing tasks by reasonably allocating limited wireless communication and edge computing resources in each time slot' (p. 5, problem P1; p. 1: 'joint optimization of wireless and edge computing resources'). This is MEC edge computing resource allocation plus per-task bandwidth scheduling, which the instructions place above the physical layer. Moving tasks between the waiting and execution queues is a fixed priority rule, not learned (p. 7, Algorithm 1). No physical-layer decision is learned jointly. Transmit powers are fixed at 27 and 30 dBm (p. 8). title: Over-the-Air Federated Learning Under Time-Varying Wireless Channels Using OTFS
q1_support: p. 5: "The simulations are performed with an extended vehicular A (EVA) model." EVA is a standardized 3GPP LTE profile outside the listed models; see notes.

function: Over-the-air aggregation of FedAvg local weight vectors over OTFS, using zero-forcing delay-Doppler precoding, optimal per-device power allocation, and EKF channel tracking to cut CSI exchange (pp. 1, 4).
system: Five mobile IoT devices and one server, single-antenna (scalar delay-Doppler channel, p. 3); OTFS uplink, M=32, N=64, 3.75 kHz spacing (p. 5); no RIS; band not stated.
method: Federated learning (FedAvg) of an unspecified classification model; aggregation uses a closed-form zero-forcing precoder, Lagrangian power allocation, and an extended Kalman filter, none learned (pp. 4-5).
data_channel: Simulated extended vehicular A (EVA) channel, parameters from [14], Gauss-Markov path-gain evolution (pp. 4-5); task data: MATLAB nnet toolbox synthetic handwritten digits 0-4 (p. 5).
test_conditions: Training and testing share one simulated five-device setting; separate FedAvg runs per maximum velocity (120, 200 km/h) and SNR (10-50 dB); channel MSE for gamma 0.9, 0.995 (p. 5).
baselines: FedAvg over OFDM (conventional OTA-FL, no reference given) and FedAvg over an ideal no-fading channel as upper bound; no baseline for the channel tracker (p. 5).
metrics: Test classification accuracy of the global model versus communication round; MSE between true and EKF-reconstructed delay-Doppler channel versus SNR (p. 5).
complexity: Orders reported: EKF O(Lk^2.4) per device, ZF precoder O(MN^2.4), optimal power O(MN); CSI shared drops from MN to 3Lk samples (p. 5).
first_notes: Reason system. The paper proposes OTA computation FL over OTFS (p. 1: "we propose an over-the-air (OTA) computation-based FL scheme suitable for time-varying wireless channels"). The problem solved is the OTA aggregation itself (ZF precoder with optimal power allocation, EKF tracking of the delay-Doppler channel), so the area would be 7, which takes precedence over area 4; the single-antenna exemption of OTFS and NTN works (areas 4 and 6) therefore does not apply. The link is single-antenna and has no RIS: the system model is a CS and K IoT devices (p. 2), the delay-Doppler input-output is ydd = sum_k Hdd,k sdd,k with sdd,k in C^(NM x 1) (p. 3, eqs. 10 and 12), and no antenna array, beamformer or RIS appears anywhere in the design or the simulation (p. 5). Multiple antennas at the server and intelligent reflecting surfaces are mentioned only in related work [9] and [8] (p. 1). Learning is only the FedAvg classifier on 10,000 synthetic MATLAB digit images (p. 5); the ZF precoder, the power allocation and the EKF are not learned, but OTA FL passes the no_learning check by rule. Quantitative simulation results exist (p. 5, Fig. 2), so the results check is not the reason. Reviewer: confirm the reading that the OTFS exemption follows the area (4 and 6) and not the waveform; if the exemption is read by waveform, the work would be included as area 7.
second_notes: Over-the-air FL work: the precoder, power allocation and EKF are not learned, so it passes no_learning only through the over-the-air FL rule. Area 7 rather than 4 because the problem solved is the over-the-air aggregation itself and the main metric is global accuracy. The server and devices are single-antenna (scalar channel, p. 3; p. 1 contrasts with the multi-antenna server of [9]); kept because OTFS works admit single-antenna links. Reviewer: confirm this exception covers an area-7 OTFS work; otherwise the reason is system. q1: EVA, the extended vehicular A profile standardized by 3GPP for LTE (TS 36.101/36.104), is not among the listed models; the paper does not name 3GPP, and path gains also follow a Gauss-Markov evolution (p. 4). Reviewer to confirm. Fig. 2 legends (p. 5, read from the page image): Proposed Scheme (OTFS), FedAvg over OFDM, Ideal Channel. Carrier frequency not stated. Title and DOI on p. 1 match.

The learned parts are a DDQN policy that, at each step, activates the radar or the communication function ('a vehicle can selectively activate either the radar or the communication function based on environmental states', p. 2), picks the message type (CAM or DENM) and a rate level (pp. 4, 6), and ADMM-Net, a deep-unfolded matrix completion of missing weather, traffic and ACK states (pp. 7-8: 'we use ADMM-Net to accurately complete the missing environmental states, and then use DDQN to solve the problem'); this is scheduling and environment-state completion above the physical layer. The physical layer is abstracted: the channel is a quality level from 1 to 10 (p. 5: 'it is abstracted as the channel quality level'), the environment variables 'are represented as an abstract hazard level' built from a US accident dataset (p. 9), the radar has two fixed modes (p. 9), and no antenna array, beam, waveform design, RIS or channel estimation appears in the paper's own model. Borderline for the reviewer: if the radar-mode and rate-level choices are counted as physical-layer decisions learned jointly with the scheduling, the work passes above_phy and would then be excluded as function (link adaptation and radar-mode choice are not among the seven areas) or, read as area 5, as system (scalar SINR link, no antenna array or RIS, p. 4). title: Blockchain-Based AR Offloading in UAV-Enabled MEC Networks: A Trade-Off Between Energy Consumption and Rendering Latency
function: Excluded (above_phy): PPO learns UAV placement, the AR rendering (task offloading) decision and block-producer selection; bandwidth and computing allocation is solved by a non-learned Lagrangian method (p. 7).
first_notes: Excluded, above_phy. p. 7: the PPO action space comprises "the UAV location, the block producer decision, and the rendering decision", that is UAV placement and task offloading, both above the physical layer. Bandwidth and computing allocation (CBRA) is solved by the non-learned LMI algorithm (p. 7, Algorithm 1 on p. 8), and p. 12 says the LMI "reduces the decision space" of the DRL. No learned MIMO, RIS or other physical-layer function. PDF title and DOI match on p. 1.
second_notes: Excluded at Step 1, check 4 (above_phy). Check 3 (no_learning) does not apply because a learned PPO-based DRL agent is the primary routine of the method, but it acts above the physical layer. p. 7: "To solve the URBS problem, the PPO algorithm is adopted", where URBS is the "UAV development, rendering decision, and block producer selection"; p. 7: "The action space in the system comprises three primary elements, i.e., the UAV location, the block producer decision, and the rendering decision." The rendering decision is a task-offloading/edge-computing split (p. 5: "the proportion of the original AR tasks that UAV m needs to process"), UAV location is UAV placement, and block-producer selection is blockchain consensus management. The only physical-layer-like decision, the OFDMA bandwidth allocation of the UAV-to-user downlink, is not learned: p. 7: "For the CBRA problem, we design a Lagrangian Multiplier Iterative (LMI)-based algorithm"; p. 8, Algorithm 1: "Calculate bm,um by using Newton’s method". So the aerial-link exception (learned resource allocation counts as physical layer) does not apply. Although p. 7 says the DRL "can learn the optimal CBRA strategy from the environment", bandwidth and CPU frequencies are not in the action space; the LMI solver is embedded in the DRL environment. Tables I (p. 4) and II (p. 10), read from the page images, show no learned physical-layer decision. Page 1 holds the title "Blockchain-Based AR Offloading in UAV-Enabled MEC Networks: A Trade-Off Between Energy Consumption and Rendering Latency" and DOI 10.1109/TVT.2025.3581015, so the PDF matches the DOI.

title: Access Control in Satellite–Terrestrial Backhaul Network: An Emergent Communication Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
q1_support: Corrected by the author (own free-space and Rician backhaul model with 3GPP parameters, and own Rayleigh access link): p. 4: the backhaul is "a widely used BS-satellite backhaul channel model [30], [31], which includes free-space path loss and Rician small-scale fading", and the access link has Rayleigh fading; p. 10 cites 3GPP [48], [49] for the parameters of this backhaul
q2_support: p. 12: "under varying traffic loads, different numbers of power levels, and varying total BS-satellite backhaul channel bandwidths". No policy trained in one setting is said to be tested in another; the 30-UE cases (p. 14) are training curves.
q3_support: p. 10: "we compare it with conventional Q-Mix and independent Q-learning (IQL) algorithms" (learned); p. 11: "a reference policy called maxSINR" (non-learned). Compared on packet delay and throughput (p. 12).
q4_support: p. 10: "the overall time complexity for the execution phase is" an analytic expression in GRU, message, aggregation and Q-network sizes (Sec. V-E); the mixing network cost is given for training.
q5_support: p. 9: "we construct an offline discrete-time simulated environment for neural network training". The data come from the authors' own simulator; the paper gives no code or data link and uses no public dataset.
function: Learns each UE's uplink transmit power level, subchannel and serving-BS association (access control) in a satellite-backhauled network to minimize average packet delay (p. 5).
system: 4 BSs, 10 UEs, 2 subchannels (2 GHz); LEO satellite at 550 km, 30 GHz backhaul; no antenna arrays or RIS modelled (p. 10-11).
method: EC-MARL: QMIX value-decomposition MARL with GRU, attention-aggregated learned cooperation messages (emergent communication); centralized training, decentralized execution; DDQN-style reinforcement learning (p. 7-9).
data_channel: Offline simulator: UE-BS path loss with Rayleigh fading; BS-satellite backhaul 'specified by the 3GPP' (TR 38.821, 38.811) with Rician fading; random-waypoint UEs (p. 4, 10).
test_conditions: Trained offline in the simulator; 20 test runs under varied traffic load, power levels, backhaul bandwidth; 30-UE case shown as training curves; no unseen-condition test (p. 9, 12-14).
baselines: Learned: conventional Q-Mix, IQL (independent DDQN learners). Non-learned: maxSINR, each UE picks the highest-SINR BS at maximum power (p. 10-11).
metrics: Average packet delay, average sum throughput, and episode return (convergence) versus traffic load, power levels, backhaul bandwidth, and message dimension (p. 11-13).
complexity: Analytic time complexity of the execution phase (GRU Jl(T k^2) plus message, aggregation and Q networks) and mixing network for training; no runtime or parameter count (p. 10).
first_notes: Included, area 6, borderline. Learned actions are UE transmit power level, subchannel and BS association (p. 5): power and subchannel choice is physical-layer control learned jointly with association, so above_phy does not apply. The controlled links are terrestrial UE-BS uplinks and the satellite backhaul has fixed power and equal bandwidth shares (p. 4), so the NTN fit is for the reviewer to confirm. q1 rests only on the p. 10 statement that the backhaul follows 3GPP TR 38.811/38.821, while eq. (3) and (5) on p. 4 are free-space loss with Rayleigh and Rician fading: reviewer to confirm. q3: Q-Mix is the proposed method without emergent communication (ablation-like), so the learned baseline rests on IQL (DDQN) and Q-Mix as a published algorithm [35]. PDF title and DOI match on p. 1.

title: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface for High-Speed Railway MIMO Communication System: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
q1_support: p. 4: "following the Saleh-Valenzuela channel model". Gains are complex Gaussian with path loss and shadow fading (p. 5); a custom simulator, no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is mentioned.
q2_support: p. 11: "observing the effect of changing the velocity of the HST-MR and the number of reflecting elements of the RISs". Sweeps only; no model trained in one setting is said to be tested in another, and transfer learning is future work (p. 15).
q3_support: p. 15: "its advantage over the modified benchmark URBR-DDPG algorithm". The only baseline is the learned URBR-DDPG; FP and WMMSE are only named on p. 2 and no non-learned method is compared in Figs. 15-18.
q4_support: p. 10: "The overall training complexity (time complexity) for the URBR-DDPG algorithm can be formulated as" an O(.) expression; PBPR and RBPR are given likewise, and Table I (p. 11) lists measured step and training times.
q5_support: p. 5: "the time-varying channel gain which follows a complex Gaussian distribution similar to that used in [14]". Data come from the authors' own simulator; the paper gives no code or data link and uses no public dataset.
function: DDPG actor jointly outputs BS beamforming and the phase shifts of two RISs to maximize downlink spectral efficiency at the train mobile relay (p. 6).
system: Downlink MIMO in a tunnel: BS 8 antennas, train relay 8 antennas, two reflecting RISs of 16 elements, 28 GHz mmWave, 350 km/h (p. 4, 11).
method: DDPG with proportional (PBPR) and rank-based (RBPR) prioritized experience replay on TD error; actor-critic with two hidden layers; reinforcement learning trained off-line (p. 7-9).
data_channel: Custom simulator: Saleh-Valenzuela mmWave paths, Gaussian gains with path loss and shadow fading, Doppler, outdated CSI via Jakes' correlation; no standard model or dataset (p. 4-5).
test_conditions: 15000 episodes of 50 steps at 350 km/h, 16 elements per RIS; SE also reported at 50 and 600 km/h and 9-49 elements; retraining unstated (p. 11, 14-15).
baselines: URBR-DDPG (uniform replay DDPG adapted from [14]) only; FP and WMMSE are named in the introduction but not compared (p. 2, 13-14).
metrics: Instantaneous and average spectral efficiency (bps/Hz), actor loss, training stability; SE versus velocity and RIS elements; step and episode duration (p. 11-15).
complexity: Training time complexity per algorithm in O(.) form, inference and memory complexity; measured step, episode and total training time on GPU and CPU (Table I) (p. 10-11).
first_notes: Included, area 3: DDPG variants learn the BS beamformer and the phase shifts of two RISs (p. 6). q3=0 because the only baseline is URBR-DDPG, itself a learned method. q4=1 from the complexity analysis (p. 9-10) and measured runtimes (Table I, p. 11). Retraining per velocity or RIS size is not stated, and the RIS-size sweep changes the action dimension, so q2=0. PDF title and DOI match on p. 1.

title: Near-Field Beam Training and Tracking With Deep Learning for Extremely Large-Scale MIMO
q1_support: p. 4: "we generate the dataset by simulations", after "the existing real world trajectory datasets cannot provide the denoised channel". Custom near-field simulator with one LoS and two NLoS paths; no 3GPP, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 4: "the dataset has 50,000 entries, with 80% of data used for training and 20% of data used" for testing; p. 5: "we evaluate the LNBT with T = 2, 3". Held-out split of the same simulated distribution plus SNR and T sweeps; nothing states a trained model meets an unseen scenario.
q3_support: p. 5: "the original scheme [9], the improved scheme [9], and the hierarchical scheme [8]" compared on normalized gain (Fig. 4) and achievable rate (Fig. 5); p. 6: [9] is "Deep learning based beam training for extremely large-scale massive MIMO in near-field domain". [8] and beam sweeping are non-learned.
q4_support: p. 4: "complexity of the mth hidden layer can be denoted as" O(...); the total orders of CTNBT and LNBT are then given in terms of N(1), Ne, T, layer sizes and kernel sizes.
q5_support: p. 4: "we generate the dataset by simulations". No link or DOI to code or data is given, and no public dataset is used.
function: Near-field beam training (codeword prediction with angle and distance) and beam tracking for XL-MIMO analog beamforming; CNN predicts the best codeword, LSTM tracks it, pp. 2-4.
system: Downlink XL-MIMO: BS with 512-antenna half-wavelength ULA and analog beamforming, single-antenna UE, 50 GHz mmWave, near-field; no RIS, pp. 1, 4.
method: Supervised learning, offline: two-stage CNN with inception blocks classifying the optimal codeword (cross-entropy); CNN plus LSTM for tracking, pp. 3-4.
data_channel: Self-generated simulated dataset of 50,000 samples: near-field channel with one LoS and two NLoS paths, UE angle U(-90,90) degrees, distance U(13,100) m; no real data, p. 4.
test_conditions: Offline training on 80% of the simulated set, testing on the held-out 20% from the same distribution; SNR 0-15 dB; tracking T=10 periods, speeds U(3,17) m/s, pp. 4-5.
baselines: Non-learned: hierarchical spatial-chirp scheme [8], exhaustive beam sweeping upper bound. Learned: original and improved DL schemes [9]. Ablation: CTNBT with standard CNN block, pp. 5-6.
metrics: Normalized gain, achievable rate (bps/Hz), beam training overhead (codewords tested), effect of tracking length T, pp. 5-6.
complexity: Asymptotic order O(.) of CTNBT and LNBT in layer sizes, kernel sizes, batch size and codebook sizes; no runtime or FLOPs, p. 4.
openness: none; dataset generated by simulation, no code or data link, p. 4.
first_notes: Included, area 3: the learned method selects and tracks the beam (codeword) and is judged by normalized gain and achievable rate; the angle and distance of the UE are a by-product, not a localization task. [9] is taken as learned from its title in the reference list (p. 6). q2 is borderline: Fig. 6 (p. 5) sweeps T=2 to 20 while p. 4 sets T=10 for the dataset, but the paper does not say whether the LSTM is reused or retrained, so 0.

title: Generative AI-Empowered Resilient Adaptive ISAC Against Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks
function: Excluded (function): the learned KSGAN discriminator only detects adversarial range-Doppler maps (AML attack detection, p. 11); no beams, waveforms, or resources are learned.
first_notes: Reason function. The only learned component is the KSGAN discriminator (convolution and max pooling blocks, p. 10) that decides whether a received range-Doppler map is genuine or adversarial: p. 11: "tasked with detecting whether there is an AML attack". This is a security detection function, close to the excluded physical-layer authentication and anti-jamming, and it is not one of the seven areas. The switch between ISAC and communication-only transmission, the sensing power share alpha_sen* in {0.5, 0}, and the sensing beam gate alpha_beam are fixed threshold rules on the detector output and on the 2D CFAR result (Eqs. 22-23, p. 11; Eq. 25, p. 12), not learned. BORDERLINE: the abstract (p. 1) frames the adaptive transmission as ISAC resource allocation: "To optimize resource allocation in ISAC systems, we propose an adaptive signal transmission method", so the reviewer may reconsider area 5. Facts for that case: 2 Tx and 2 Rx antennas at the vehicle, 2 or 6 single-antenna users, 77 GHz, no RIS (Table II, p. 13); custom MATLAB and IBM ART simulation of 3000 legitimate range-Doppler maps, no 3GPP channel, no code link (p. 13); no complexity figure reported.
second_notes: Page 1 holds the title and DOI 10.1109/TVT.2025.3583924, so the PDF is this paper. Step 1: a research article (not code 1) that proposes and evaluates a method (not 2); learning is central (p. 9: "To detect AML attacks, we designed a unique GAN that is trained with a differentiable KS loss function"), so not 3; the learning acts on the radar Range-Doppler map, not above the PHY (not 4). Code 5 applies: the learned model only classifies Range-Doppler maps as real or adversarial (p. 10: "The discriminator is tasked with detecting whether there is an AML attack"; Fig. 5, p. 9), a security function akin to the excluded physical-layer authentication and anti-jamming. No learned component outputs beams, waveforms, or resources: the sensing/communication power split and the sensing-beam on/off are fixed threshold rules on the detector output (p. 10, eqs. 22-23; p. 12, eq. 25), the communication precoder is closed form (p. 5: "We employ Regularized Zero-Forcing (RZF) precoding"), the mode-switch period comes from a Poisson model (p. 12), and range and velocity come from classical 2D CFAR (p. 6). Borderline for the reviewer: the paper casts detection as subproblem P1a of a weighted-CRLB resource problem (p. 8) and the detector output gates the ISAC transmission, so area 5 could be argued; I judged that the ISAC resource decision itself is not learned. Not graded.

title: Optimizing Codebook Design in mmWave Massive MIMO Using Digital Twin-Assisted DRL
q1_support: p. 10: "were simulated based on the DeepMIMO dataset [39]". The three scenarios O1_60, I2_28B and I3_60 of Table I are DeepMIMO scenarios.
q2_support: p. 12: "in the LoS, NLoS, and LoS&NLoS scenarios". Not met: each scenario gets its own site-specific codebook learned from scratch, and no codebook is tested outside its learning scenario; the twin validation split (p. 11) is held-out data of the same set.
q3_support: p. 14: "by codebooks learned through online DT-DRL, traditional DRL methods, and the classical beamsteering codebook (32-beam)". Both comparisons are on the average beamforming gain (Figs. 9 and 10).
q4_support: p. 13: "the online DT-DRL incurs only about 3% increase in FLOPs". Eq. (44) and Table III give FLOPs, model size and latency of the proposed method.
q5_support: p. 10: "were simulated based on the DeepMIMO dataset [39]". Public channel dataset; the paper releases no code or data of its own.
function: Learns site-specific analog beam codebooks (phase-shifter beam patterns) for the base station without CSI, using DRL agents trained inside a digital-twin environment (pp. 3-4, 7-8).
system: Downlink mmWave massive MIMO: base station with 32 antennas, one RF chain, 4-bit phase shifters; single-antenna users; 60 and 28 GHz; no RIS (pp. 3-4, 10).
method: Reinforcement learning: SAC, TD3, DDPG agents; digital twin is a fully connected network trained supervised on gain measurements; K-means clustering; online or offline (pp. 4-9).
data_channel: DeepMIMO dataset scenarios O1_60 (outdoor LoS), I2_28B (indoor NLoS), I3_60 (mixed), 5 paths; one codebook learned and evaluated per scenario on its own users (p. 10).
test_conditions: Each scenario (LoS, NLoS, LoS&NLoS) learned and evaluated separately on its own channel set; codebook sizes 4 to 16 beams; no cross-scenario test (pp. 10-13).
baselines: Non-learned: classical 32-beam beamsteering codebook. Learned: traditional DRL (DDPG, TD3, SAC) interacting with the real environment, the approach of [17], [18]; matrix-block twin (pp. 11, 14).
metrics: Normalized average beamforming gain (EGC bound), pilot overhead, FLOPs, model size, latency, and digital-twin MSE loss (pp. 11-14).
complexity: FLOPs 1152NT^2M+64NTM (DRL) vs 1184NT^2M+80NTM (DT-DRL); 4.73M vs 4.86M FLOPs, 18.08 vs 9.56 MB, latency 9.63 ms (p. 13).
openness: none of its own; p. 4 footnote 2 links the Codebook_Learning_RL repository, apparently the code of earlier work [17]; DeepMIMO is public.
first_notes: Area 3 (beam codebook design). Reviewer checks. (1) q3 counts traditional DRL (DDPG, TD3, SAC without the digital twin; the approach cited as [17], [18] on p. 2 and the code linked in the p. 4 footnote) as the earlier learned baseline. If the reviewer reads it as an ablation of the twin module, q3 becomes 0. (2) q2 is 0: p. 11 says the generalization capability is validated via multi-scenario simulation experiments, but each scenario is learned separately (site-specific) and no codebook is tested in another scenario. (3) p. 10 says the framework does not directly interface with the datasets; the DRL agent receives beamforming gains computed from the DeepMIMO channels, so q1 and q5 rest on DeepMIMO.

title: Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces and STAR-RIS-Enabled Terahertz ISAC System
q1_support: p. 3: "channel is characterized using a ray-tracing Saleh-Valenzuela". Not met: custom Saleh-Valenzuela THz channel with spreading and absorption path loss; no 3GPP model, DeepMIMO, or measured data.
q2_support: p. 5: "achieves faster and smoother convergence than other DRL methods". Not met: adaptation to unseen environments is claimed (p. 4) but no result tests a trained model on a new placement or configuration; Fig. 2 shows convergence and EE sweeps only.
q3_support: p. 5: "we compare it with benchmark algorithms: Meta-SAC, SAC, and PPO". Not met: all three are learned (Meta-SAC is the method without the GAN), compared by reward convergence (Fig. 2a); no non-learned baseline.
q4_support: p. 5: "The complexity analysis of the proposed GAN-based Meta-SAC algorithm can be divided into three parts". Eqs. (11)-(13) give the order of complexity of training and running.
q5_support: p. 5: "Additional SIM parameters align with [3] and Meta-SAC training follows [18]". Not met: parameters are listed, but no code or data link and no public dataset; the channel is simulated (p. 3).
function: Jointly optimizes BS power allocation, SIM phase shifts, and STAR-RIS transmission-reflection coefficients to maximize energy efficiency under per-user rate and CRB sensing constraints (pp. 1, 4).
system: 0.1 THz ISAC; 8-antenna ULA BS with stacked SIM (4 layers, 16 atoms); STAR-RIS, simultaneously transmitting and reflecting (25 elements, 5 sensors); 4 single-antenna users, 4 targets (pp. 2, 5).
method: Meta-reinforcement learning: soft actor-critic with MAML meta-training and meta-adaptation, plus a GAN in the critic modeling state-action value distributions (pp. 4-5).
data_channel: Simulated THz channel: ray-tracing Saleh-Valenzuela SIM-to-STAR-RIS model with spatial correlation, spreading and absorption path loss; users and targets placed randomly; no external dataset (pp. 3, 5).
test_conditions: Meta-training on tasks of user and target placements; adaptation to unseen ones claimed (pp. 4-5); reported: convergence and EE sweeps over CRB bound, power, SIM size, sensors (p. 5).
baselines: Learned only: Meta-SAC (the proposed method without GAN), SAC, and PPO; no non-learned baseline (p. 5).
metrics: Energy efficiency and training reward; sensing accuracy enters only through the CRB threshold, varied in Fig. 2(b) (p. 5).
complexity: Big-O expressions for GAN training, Meta-SAC training, and running mode, and their sum; no numerical operations count or runtime (p. 5).
first_notes: Letter. Area 5 rather than 3: the learned Meta-SAC sets power, SIM phase shifts and STAR-RIS coefficients under a CRB sensing constraint, an ISAC beam and resource problem, and ISAC outranks area 3. Reviewer checks. (1) q2 is 0 because adaptation to unseen environments is claimed (p. 4: "enabling the agent to adapt quickly to unseen environments") but no test on new placements or configurations is reported; if Fig. 2(a) is read as meta-adaptation to new tasks, q2 could be 1. (2) q3 is 0 for lack of any non-learned baseline; Meta-SAC is an ablation of the proposed method. (3) q4 rests on the symbolic big-O formulas of Section III-C (p. 5); no numbers or runtime.

title: Cooperative Beam Management for Neighboring LEO Satellites Without Ground Control
q1_support: p. 2: "this paper adopts the Rician fading model to characterize the communication channel". Not met: Rician fading with parameters from [12], free-space path loss and Poisson traffic are custom; 3GPP TR 38.811 is cited only for the multi-beam antenna pattern; no standard channel, dataset, or measurement.
q2_support: p. 5: "under increasing communication demand". Not met: throughput is swept over demand and cache queue length (Figs. 3 and 4); the paper never states that a model trained under one setting is tested under another.
q3_support: p. 4: "NCS-DRL Algorithm [16]: Single satellite beam hopping based on deep reinforcement learning". Non-learned Random, NSBC-Greedy [15] and DBSO [6] are listed on the same page; all five methods are compared on throughput (Fig. 3a, p. 5).
q4_support: p. 5: "the total online computational complexity of the". Eqs. (15)-(18) give the operation count as a sum over layers of W_{l-1}*W_l*delta^2 for the actor and policy networks, times the number of beams.
q5_support: p. 4: "The key link parameters are summarized in Table I, partially adapted from [4]". Not met: custom Python simulation with parameters in Table I; no link to code or data and no public dataset.
function: Learns per-time-slot beam illumination (which cell each beam serves) for two neighboring LEO satellites with full frequency reuse to maximize throughput, without ground control (pp. 1, 3).
system: 2 LEO satellites (780 km), Ka-band 20 GHz, 500 MHz; phased arrays, 10 beams and 37 cells each, 10 cells overlap, full frequency reuse; no RIS (pp. 1, 4).
method: Multi-agent DRL, actor-critic with centralized critic and one actor per beam, plus policy-approximation networks inferring other agents; centralized offline training, distributed onboard inference (pp. 1, 3-4).
data_channel: Simulated: free-space path loss, Rician fading with elevation-dependent parameters from [12], 3GPP TR 38.811 multi-beam antenna pattern, Poisson packet arrivals per cell; no dataset (pp. 2, 4).
test_conditions: Training converges near iteration 500 (3600 steps each, Fig. 2); evaluation sweeps demand 400-2400 Mbps and queue length 2-7; no separate training and test conditions stated (pp. 4-5).
baselines: Non-learned: Random, NSBC-Greedy [15], DBSO [6]. Learned: NCS-DRL [16], single-satellite DRL beam hopping, non-cooperative (p. 4).
metrics: Normalized reward, system throughput (Mbps), and probability of cell illumination; throughput vs demand and cache queue length (pp. 4-5).
complexity: Online operation count: sum of W_{l-1}*W_l*delta^2 over layers for actor and policy networks, times K_tot beams (Eqs. 15-18); no numeric value (p. 5).
first_notes: Area 6: learned control of beams in satellite links (beam illumination per cell and slot), so it passes the above-PHY check by the satellite exception, although the paper also models cell queues and traffic. Reviewer checks. (1) q1 is 0: 3GPP TR 38.811 is cited only for the multi-beam antenna pattern (p. 2), while fading (Rician, [12]), path loss and traffic are custom; if the reviewer counts the antenna pattern as a TR 38.811 model, q1 becomes 1. (2) q3 counts NCS-DRL [16], a published DRL beam-hopping scheme, as the learned baseline; the paper attributes the gap to the policy approximation network (p. 4), so it could be read as an ablation. (3) q4 rests on the operation-count formulas of Section IV-C (p. 5), no numeric value.

title: Joint Power Control and Precoding for Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems With Sparse Multi-Dimensional Graph Neural Networks
q1_support: p. 3: "channels modeled by Rayleigh fading and large-scale fading" with a path-loss formula, and "modeled by the SV model with Ncl = 4 clusters, Nray = 5 rays"; a custom simulator, no 3GPP, DeepMIMO or measured data is named.
q2_support: p. 3: "Datasets include 10,000 training and 2,000 testing samples." Test samples come from the same simulated setting; no unseen scenario, antenna or user number is reported.
q3_support: p. 4: "We compare it with three methods under identical conditions: the baseline MDGNN, the attention-based MDGNN (A-MDGNN), and the WMMSE algorithm." SE is compared in Fig. 4 and Fig. 5(a).
q4_support: p. 5: "The computational complexity comparison presented here is based on measuring the computation time required to process an identical number of samples using the same hardware setup for each method."
q5_support: p. 3: "Datasets include 10,000 training and 2,000 testing samples." The data are simulated by the authors; no code or data link or availability statement appears anywhere in the paper.
function: Learned joint power control and precoding for cell-free massive MIMO APs, maximizing sum spectral efficiency, with learned pruning of weak AP-UE links to cut complexity (p. 1-3).
system: Cell-free massive MIMO: power control L=9 APs with 8 antennas, K=8 single-antenna UEs; precoding K=4 UEs, Nt=16 antennas; no RIS; frequency band not stated (p. 2-3).
method: Sparse multi-dimensional GNN: learnable sigmoid adjacency and threshold mask prune weak links; power-control and precoding heads; end-to-end SE-maximizing loss (unsupervised in effect, not named) (p. 3).
data_channel: Simulated: Rayleigh fading with large-scale fading -30.5-36.7log10(d) for power control; SV model (4 clusters, 5 rays, 10 degrees spread) for precoding; 10,000 training, 2,000 test samples (p. 3).
test_conditions: Train on 10,000 samples, test on 2,000 of the same simulated setting with perfect CSI; threshold tau swept 0.5-0.7; no other scenario tested (p. 3-4).
baselines: Non-learned: WMMSE algorithm; learned: baseline MDGNN [12] and attention-based MDGNN (A-MDGNN), compared on SE and computation time (p. 3-5).
metrics: Sum spectral efficiency (CDF, relative SE), computation time relative to MDGNN, sparsity, performance retention and their harmonic mean (p. 4-5).
complexity: Measured computation time for identical samples and hardware: SP-MDGNN 0.52 times MDGNN, 48% reduction (55% power control, 49% precoding); WMMSE 25.29 times (Fig. 5, p. 4-5).
first_notes: Read all 5 pages and pages 4-5 as images (Figs. 3-5). Included: correspondence that proposes and evaluates a learned method for power control and precoding in cell-free massive MIMO; physical layer; simulation results; APs have several antennas. Area 3: the network output is the transmission matrix F, whose norm sets power and whose direction sets the beam (p. 2-3). q1 is 0 because the channel is the authors' own Rayleigh/SV simulator with a path-loss formula and no standardized or measured source (p. 4). q2 is 0: only one train/test split per task is reported; the sentence on p. 5 about robustness 'validated across a myriad of network conditions' is not backed by any reported experiment. q3 is borderline: WMMSE is the classical baseline and MDGNN [12] is a published learned method ('the original MDGNN method', p. 1), but SP-MDGNN extends MDGNN, so the reviewer may read it as an ablation, in which case q3 would be 0; A-MDGNN is an attention variant and is not counted. q4 rests on measured computation time (p. 5, Fig. 5b). PDF is arXiv v1 (2 Jul 2025) of 'Joint Power Control and Precoding for Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems With Sparse Multi-Dimensional Graph Neural Networks'; the DOI-title match could not be checked with the allowed files.
published_notes: Included, area 3 (precoder and power control of cell-free APs). It is a correspondence but proposes and evaluates a method with results. q3 counted as met with WMMSE as the non-learned baseline and MDGNN [12] as an earlier published learned method, although MDGNN is also the non-sparse base of SP-MDGNN; reviewer to confirm. title: Standards-Compliant DM-RS Allocation via Temporal Channel Prediction for Massive MIMO Systems
q1_support: p. 3: "ray-tracing module of NVIDIA Sionna" and "We employed the simple_street_canyon_with_cars scene"; Sionna's public ray tracer and built-in scene, not 3GPP or DeepMIMO (reviewer to confirm).
q2_support: p. 3: "split into training/validation/test sets with an 8: 1: 1 ratio"; p. 4: "We evaluated each scheme over SNRs" from -10 to 15 dB. Held-out split and SNR sweep only; no new scene, band, array, or speed.
q3_support: p. 4: "DRL [24]: A CNN-based deep Q-network" (learned) and "Maximize Data Symbols: A heuristic scheme" plus "Random Average" (non-learned), compared on accuracy and throughput.
q4_support: p. 3: "The ViViT complexity is O(L(N 2 D + N D2 ))"; footnote 1 gives about 1.082e9 FLOPs ("the ViViT model requires") and about 3.47 us on an A100.
q5_support: p. 3: "yielding 6,000 slots in total"; the dataset is generated by the authors with Sionna ray tracing; no code or data link or DOI appears anywhere in the paper.
function: Classifies the optimal DM-RS allocation (1 of 13 NR patterns) for the next slot from uplink CSI, jointly with channel prediction, without CSI feedback (pp. 1-2).
system: Massive MIMO FDD OFDM downlink: BS 8x8 array, UE 2x1 array, no RIS; NR band n1 (UL 1.95 GHz, DL 2.14 GHz), 100 MHz bandwidth (p. 3).
method: ViViT (spatial and temporal transformer encoders) and 3D-CNN classifiers over 13 allocations, trained end to end with supervision on exhaustive-search labels (pp. 2-4).
data_channel: Sionna ray tracing, scene simple_street_canyon_with_cars, UE at 60-80 km/h; Gaussian error (~0.05) added; 6,000 slots split 8:1:1 into train, validation, test (p. 3).
test_conditions: Same scene and speeds for training and test; held-out 10% split, 250 test slots; SNR swept -10 to 15 dB, training SNR not stated (pp. 3-4).
baselines: Learned: DRL (CNN-based DQN [24]), Disjoint ViViT/CNN predictor [22] plus pilot pruning [23]; non-learned: Maximize Data Symbols heuristic, Random Average; oracle Best (p. 4).
metrics: Allocation classification accuracy per SNR (Table II), average data throughput and gain over second-best benchmark (Fig. 4), NMSE of the disjoint channel predictor (pp. 4-5).
complexity: ViViT O(L(N^2 D + N D^2)); 3D-CNN O(L F C K^3 HWT); ViViT with L=8, N=64, D=128 needs about 1.082e9 FLOPs, about 3.47 us on A100 (p. 3).
first_notes: Step 1 in order: a 5-page research letter (not an editorial), not a survey, a learned component exists (ViViT/CNN classifier, p. 3), and it acts on the physical layer (DM-RS), so the function check decides. p. 2: 'the proposed CPRS framework directly classifies the optimal allocation' from the uplink CSI, among '|P| = 13 possible allocations'; the labels come from an exhaustive search of throughput (p. 4). The proposed model outputs no channel estimate, compressed CSI or predicted channel; the channel predictor with NMSE -8.42 dB (p. 4) belongs only to the 'Disjoint' baseline. Reported metrics are allocation accuracy (Table II, p. 4) and throughput (Fig. 4, p. 5). Choosing the DM-RS pattern is a reference-signal configuration decision of the link-adaptation type, which is outside the seven areas. BORDERLINE: the paper frames CPRS as channel-prediction-based and as a way to reduce CSI feedback (p. 1), so the reviewer may reassign it to area 2. Facts for a reassignment: Sionna ray tracing of the street-canyon-with-cars scene, 8x8 BS array, 2x1 UE, band n1, random 8:1:1 split with no unseen condition (p. 4); baselines DRL [24], Disjoint ViViT/CNN, Maximize Data Symbols, Random Average (p. 4); ViViT complexity O(L(N^2 D + N D^2)) and about 1.082e9 FLOPs (pp. 3-4); no code or data link. The PDF is the arXiv 2507.11064v2 preprint (p. 1) and carries no DOI.
second_notes: PDF is arXiv 2507.11064v2; its title and authors match the Crossref record of the DOI (IEEE TVT, 2026). Eligibility borderline on function: the network outputs a DM-RS (pilot) time pattern, not a channel estimate, and channel prediction is implicit (p. 2: 'directly classifies the optimal allocation'). I read it as pilot allocation for channel estimation and CSI-feedback reduction, area 2 (pp. 1-2); if the reviewer takes adaptive DM-RS selection as link adaptation, the code would be function. q1: channels come from Sionna RT ray tracing on the public built-in scene simple_street_canyon_with_cars (p. 4), not one of the listed models; marked met for the reviewer to confirm as a public ray-tracing source. q5 stays 0 even if q1 is confirmed, since the generated channels (placement, trajectories, Gaussian augmentation) are neither released nor fully specified. q3: DQN [24] is a standard algorithm applied to the same problem; the disjoint baseline combines published learned methods [22], [23] with the CPRS backbone settings. CPRS (CNN) is a second backbone of the proposed method, not a baseline. q4: the 3.47 µs is computed from FLOPs and the A100 peak rate, not measured.
published_notes: Borderline function: the learned classifier picks the DM-RS pattern from uplink CSI jointly with downlink channel prediction (abstract, p. 1; Sec. II, p. 2), counted as area 2; a reviewer could instead see link adaptation. Supervised paradigm inferred from classification on exhaustive-search labels (p. 3); the word is not used. q1: Sionna RT with its built-in public scene, marked met for confirmation. q5 is 0 because the generated channels and labels are not released. The check of the first page shows the title Standards-Compliant DM-RS Allocation via Temporal Channel Prediction for Massive MIMO Systems, matching the DOI.

title: UAV-Enabled Data Collection for IoT Networks via Rainbow Learning

Receive beamforming in RLA is solved by SCA, not learned (p. 4). Area 6: power, resource and beam control of a UAV link. q3 is borderline: the DDQN benchmark is the ALO scheme with DDQN in place of FDQN (p. 5), and FBS is not described beyond its name; accepted as a standard-algorithm baseline and a fixed-beam baseline, reviewer to confirm. No comparison with an earlier published method. The PDF is the arXiv 2409.14521v2 preprint (p. 1).
published_notes: Eligibility: learned GN transmit power (and beam codebook in ALO) is physical layer in an aerial link, learned jointly with UAV trajectory and scheduling (p. 3), so the above_phy check passes; area 6. RLA beamforming is SCA, not learned (p. 4). FBS is only named (p. 5); a reader who takes it as a fixed non-learned scheme would grade q3 as 1 through DDQN plus FBS. Title on p. 1 matches the DOI. title: Meta Reinforcement Learning Empowered Orchestration of SIM and RIS for Downlink Multiuser Communications

title: Area Restoration of Channel Impulse Response With Time Decomposition Based Super-Resolution Method
function: Excluded as system: learned CIR spatial super-resolution (BiLSTM plus BasicVSR) on single-antenna links, one transmitting antenna and omnidirectional receiving points, no RIS (p. 9, p. 4).
first_notes: Checks 1 to 5 pass: research article (TWC 2024, title on p. 1 matches the DOI), proposes and evaluates a learned method (p. 9), and the learned function is spatial prediction or synthesis of the channel, an area 2 type problem: "the problem of CIR super-resolution is estimating the unknown {yi,j,t } given {xi,j,t } are known" (p. 5). Check 6 (system) applies: "In each scenario, one transmitting antenna is deployed, and 256 × 256 receiving points" (p. 9); "each antenna elements has been considered as an ideal omni-directional antenna" (p. 4); the CIR h(t) is the response between one transmitting antenna and one receiving antenna (p. 1, p. 4). The receiving points are positions over an area of about 89 m by 139 m (p. 9), not a MIMO array, and no MIMO channel matrix is modelled. No RIS or reflecting surface appears anywhere in the paper. MIMO and "multi-antenna wireless channel characterizations" appear only as motivation (p. 1). If the reviewer rejects the area 2 reading of the function (radio-map or channel-modelling task rather than channel estimation), the first code that applies would be function instead of system. For reference: ray-tracing dataset of London outdoor scenes at 28 GHz, 467 training and 454 test scenarios (p. 8), compared with bilinear and bicubic interpolation and image and video super-resolution models (p. 10), MSE_dB 31.14 dB on test (p. 10).
second_notes: Reason code 6 (system), shown on p. 9: "In each scenario, one transmitting antenna is deployed, and 256 × 256 receiving points with a height of 2 m from the ground are set". Each receiving point is a single antenna, p. 4: "each antenna elements has been considered as an ideal omni-directional antenna", and each CIR is a scalar, p. 4: "a deterministic complex scalar"; Fig. 2(a), p. 5, shows one transmitting antenna and receiving antennas 1-20 at separate positions. The receiving points are spaced 0.54 m by 0.35 m over an area of about 89.1 m by 139.3 m at 28 GHz (pp. 8-9), so they are separate single-antenna receivers of a radio map, not an antenna array; MIMO appears only as motivation (pp. 1-2). No RIS, and not an OTFS or NTN work. Codes 1-5 do not apply: a research article (IEEE TWC) whose learned TDVSR model (BiLSTM time decomposition + BasicVSR, trained on SBR ray tracing) estimates the CIRs at unmeasured locations, i.e. estimation/synthesis of the channel, area 2 (p. 2: "utilize the deep learning video super-resolution model to estimate the area channel information"). The title on p. 1 matches the DOI.

title: Spectrum Breathing: Protecting Over-the-Air Federated Learning Against Interference

(5): 'hk(n) ~ CN(0, 1) represents the k-th Rayleigh fading channel coefficient' (scalar channel, scalar received chip); p. 5, eq. (13): scalar truncated channel inversion pk(n) = sqrt(P0)/hk(n) when |hk(n)|^2 >= Gth, and Fig. 2 draws one antenna at the device and one at the server; p. 9: 'one server and 10 devices' and 'all channel coefficients are modelled as CN(0, 1) random variables'. title: Satellite-Terrestrial Coordinated Multi-Satellite Beam Hopping Scheduling Based on Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning

The system check does not apply to NTN works. q2 is 1 because the paper states that the test load cases lie outside the training range (p. 11, Table IV image on p. 11), but the new conditions are traffic loads of the same constellation and channel model, so the reviewer may confirm. q1 is 0: antenna patterns follow ITU-R S.1528 and S.465-6 (p. 4) but the channel is free-space path loss in an own simulator, so the reviewer may confirm. title: Deep Learning-Based Design of Uplink Integrated Sensing and Communication
q1_support: p. 8: "The Rayleigh fading is considered" as small-scale fading; path loss "PLdB = 128.1 + 37.6 log10 (d) [30]" comes from a 3GPP CoMP document (p. 13). Custom simulator with only the path loss from 3GPP; no TR 38.901 model, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.

function: Joint design of sensing transmit waveform (learned singular values) and communication receive beamforming (closed-form recovery) for uplink ISAC, maximizing weighted normalized sensing and communication rates (pp. 6, 8).

test_conditions: Training and test samples drawn from the same random generator (8,000/2,000/2,000); sweeps over SNR, K, antennas, weight and CSI accuracy are reported; no train-test mismatch is stated (pp. 8-12).

metrics: Weighted sum of normalized sensing and communication rates (WSNR), sensing rate, communication rate, sum communication rate (bits/s/Hz), training/validation loss, runtime in ms (pp. 8-12).

title: Automatic High-Performance Neural Network Construction for Channel Estimation in IRS-Aided Communications
q1_support: p. 13: "Fig. 10 illustrates the NMSE perfomance on the DeepMIMO dataset" (outdoor ray-tracing scenario O1, 28 GHz); the main experiments use an own Rician model (p. 9).

system: TDD uplink, AP with 16 antennas, 6 single-antenna users, passive reflecting IRS with 64 elements; DeepMIMO case 64 AP antennas and 64 elements, 28 GHz (pp. 3, 9, 12).
method: Differentiable neural architecture search (CENAS) with truncated back-propagation bilevel optimization, searching a CNN denoiser (convolution, separable, dilated cells); supervised on noisy LS estimates, then retrained (pp. 5-8).

The main results (Figs. 7 to 9, p. 9 setup) use an own Rician simulator; q1 and q5 are met only through the additional experiment on DeepMIMO scenario O1 (28 GHz, LOS path excluded; Table II on p. 12, text on p. 13), whose train and test split is not detailed, so the reviewer may confirm. q2 is 0: the sweeps over SNR, N, M and pilots (pp. 11-13) do not state that a trained model is reused in a new configuration, and the paper describes generating networks of varying scale (p. 1, Table I on p. 10). q3: CDRN [16] is the earlier learned baseline and LS and LMMSE the non-learned ones; DARTS [35] is compared only on search convergence (p. 10). method: MADDPG (centralized training, distributed execution): actor-critic agents per device and UAV, shared reward equal to the negative training cost; reinforcement learning, trained over episodes (pp. 8-10).

title: Decentralized Federated Learning via MIMO Over-the-Air Computation: Consensus Analysis and Performance Optimization
q1_support: p. 9: "We model the communication channels as independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Rayleigh fading"; custom simulator, no 3GPP, DeepMIMO or COST 2100 model and no measured data.
