function: Over-the-air aggregation of local models in decentralized federated learning: joint design of transceiver beamformers and mixing matrix over MIMO full-duplex D2D links (p. 2, p. 7).
system: Ad hoc D2D network of M=30 devices, each with NT=NR=20 antennas by default, in-band full-duplex, block fading; no RIS; carrier frequency not stated (p. 4, p. 9).
method: Alternating optimization (convex QCQP and closed form for beamformers, convex program for mixing matrix); CNN trained by decentralized SGD, federated, supervised (p. 7, p. 8).
data_channel: Own i.i.d. Rayleigh fading simulator; MNIST (20k training, 10k validation samples) with a heterogeneous split over 30 devices; no standard channel model or measurement (p. 8, p. 9).
test_conditions: Training and testing share the Rayleigh model and MNIST task; results versus antennas, SNR, devices, topology sparsity; no unseen-condition test; 30 trials (p. 9, p. 10).
baselines: Joint optimization with separate OTA aggregation [39]; digital communication [40], zero-forcing [28], and MMSE beamforming [18], each with random mixing matrix; error-free case; centralized FL (p. 9, 11, 12).
metrics: Minimum and average test accuracy across devices, and communication NMSE in dB (p. 9, p. 10).
complexity: Worst-case order O(Jmax(I1max M N^3.5 + I2max M^7)) for Algorithm 2, N = NT; CNN has 21880 parameters; no runtime reported (p. 8).
first_notes: Included in area 7: the learned element is the CNN trained across devices with decentralized FL, and the problem solved is the over-the-air aggregation itself (MIMO beamformers plus mixing matrix, pp. 13-14); the physical-layer design is classical alternating optimization, which passes no_learning under the federated-learning-over-the-air rule. System check passes: NT=NR=20 antennas (p. 19). q3 is borderline: the learned-baseline role is played by the zero-forcing design of [17] adapted with a random mixing matrix, while JO with SOA (special case of the design of [37], p. 22) is close to a time-division variant of the proposed scheme (p. 7, footnote 1); the reviewer should confirm. The PDF is arXiv 2310.05075v1 (8 Oct 2023), titled Decentralized Federated Learning via MIMO Over-the-Air Computation: Consensus Analysis and Performance Optimization.
published_notes: Included under the federated-learning-over-the-air rule: the proposed design is convex alternating optimization, but the learned element is the CNN trained across devices (p. 8). Area 7, since the problem solved is the over-the-air aggregation itself (p. 2). q3 marked met on the reading that [39], [28], [40], [18] are earlier published aggregation designs; the paper adapts them (random mixing matrix, time-division version of [39], p. 11-12), so the reviewer should confirm. q4 counts the complexity of the aggregation and transceiver design.

title: Trainable Joint Channel Estimation, Detection, and Decoding for MIMO URLLC Systems
q1_support: p. 9: "the Saleh-Valenzuela model is used to generate the mmWave MIMO channel"; Gaussian channels follow the Kronecker model; custom simulators, no 3GPP, COST 2100 or DeepMIMO model and no measured data.
q2_support: p. 13: "directly applying the parameters trained under i.i.d. Gaussian channels for correlated Gaussian channels"; also "directly loaded with the parameters trained for C1 of codelength N = 288 and evaluated with C2 of codelength N = 144".
q3_support: p. 10: "The traditional decoupled and turbo receivers, including the IDD [14], [15] and the ICDD [16], are adopted for performance comparison"; all are non-learned, no earlier learned receiver is compared, and JCDD-G is the untrained variant of the proposed network.
q4_support: p. 14: "the proposed JCDD networks require only 1.1e5 operations per layer"; Table I gives the operations per codeword and Table II the CPU time.

function: Joint channel estimation, detection, and LDPC decoding of coded MIMO signals with few pilots, outputting the information bits and the channel estimate (p. 1, p. 5).
system: Coded single-carrier MIMO; Gaussian channels Nr=8, Nt=4; mmWave UPAs 2x2 transmit and 8x8 receive; short LDPC (3,6) N=288; no RIS; mmWave band, frequency not stated (p. 9).
method: Deep unfolding of ADMM receivers (JCDDNet-G, JCDDNet-S) with layer-wise trainable parameters; supervised offline training, multi-stage, Adam optimizer (p. 6, p. 10).
data_channel: Own simulators: i.i.d. Gaussian, Kronecker-correlated Gaussian, and Saleh-Valenzuela mmWave channels; 10000 training samples; no 3GPP model or measured data (p. 9, p. 10).
test_conditions: Trained at one SNR, 10000 samples; tested over SNR, then on correlated channels (0.3) and codelength 144 with i.i.d.-trained, codelength-288 parameters (p. 10, p. 13).
baselines: Decoupled, IDD and ICDD turbo receivers with MMSE, GAMP, MAP detectors; MMSE-ICDD with virtual pilot selection [17]; untrained ADMM version; no learned receiver (p. 10, p. 11).
metrics: BLER versus SNR; average iterations or layers and time per codeword; real-valued operation counts and CPU time per codeword (p. 11, p. 14).
complexity: Table I: real-valued operations per codeword (about 1.1e5 per layer, Nr=8, Nt=4); Table II: average CPU time per codeword in MATLAB (p. 14).
openness: Code at https://github.com/sunyi0101/JCDDNet (p. 10, footnote 3); channel data generated by simulation.
first_notes: Area 1 over area 2: the method solves channel estimation, detection and decoding jointly, and its main metric is the BLER of the recovered bits (Figs. 5-12) with no channel-estimation error reported; p. 3: "The ultimate goal of the receiver is to recover the information bits". Deep unfolding with trained parameters counts as learned. Generalization is shown only for mild mismatch; p. 13 admits failure for strongly deviating channel distributions or codes. The PDF is arXiv 2404.07721v1 (11 Apr 2024), titled Trainable Joint Channel Estimation, Detection and Decoding for MIMO URLLC Systems.
published_notes: Area 1 because the main metric is BLER (p. 11-13); channel estimation is joint and no channel-estimation error is reported. Deep unfolding with trained parameters counts as learned. q2 counts the direct tests with mismatched correlation and codelength (p. 13), although the paper admits failure for strongly deviated channel distributions (p. 13). Learned receivers DeepRx [23], [24] and [26] are only discussed in the introduction (p. 2), not compared, so q3 is not met.

title: Deep Learning for Efficient CSI Feedback in Massive MIMO: Adapting to New Environments and Small Datasets

function: CSI compression and recovery for downlink feedback in FDD massive MIMO, with adaptation to new scenarios by CSI translation and data augmentation (p. 1, p. 3).
system: FDD massive MIMO downlink, gNB with 32 antennas, single-antenna UEs, OFDM; no RIS; 5.3 GHz, 300 MHz, 2.61 GHz and 2.6 GHz datasets (p. 8).
method: Deep unfolding ISTA network SPTM2-ISTANet+ with trainable measurement matrix; supervised pretraining, then CNN translation module trained on few new samples (transfer); model-driven data augmentation (p. 4, p. 6).
data_channel: COST2100 indoor and outdoor, measured KU Leuven massive MIMO testbed CSI, and QuaDRiGa 3GPP TR 38.901 UMa; 100,000 training and 20,000 test samples per dataset (p. 8).
test_conditions: Pretrain on one of four datasets, test on the other three unseen, directly or with translation module trained on 200 or all samples; SNR mismatch (p. 9, 12).

title: Zero-Shot Learning for Beam Management in LEO Satellite Communications
q1_support: p. 11: "The small-scale fading follows the Rician fading model with KR = 10 dB". Custom simulator (free-space path loss, p. 3, plus Rician fading); no 3GPP, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is used.
q2_support: p. 13: "The reference angles are different from that in meta-training and meta-validation sets, and we do not have data samples in these unseen scenarios."
q3_support: p. 13: "Compared with the straightforward application of Double DQN" (learned baseline); p. 14: "the two benchmarks without machine learning, the proposed method can achieve more than 20% performance gain" (non-learned baselines).

q5_support: p. 11: "In our simulation, the mobility of the satellite, the rotation of the earth, and the random mobility of the user are considered". Data come from the authors' own simulator; the paper gives no code or data link and uses no public dataset.
function: LEO satellite beam management: GRNN predicts the next beam cell for the CSI-RS search set; Twin DQN decides when to trigger beam tracking (pp. 1, 5).
system: LEO satellite with 49x49 uniform planar array, 547-beam codebook, user receives a scalar signal (eq. 7), 11.45 GHz carrier, no RIS (pp. 3, 10-11).
method: GRNN (60 parameters) trained with supervised first-order meta-learning; Twin DQN (deep reinforcement learning) trained with meta-learning; zero-shot testing without fine-tuning (pp. 6, 10, 13).
data_channel: Custom simulator: free-space path loss plus Rician fading (KR=10 dB), Starlink-like LEO geometry, random-walk user mobility, 1000 trajectories per reference angle; no public dataset (pp. 3, 11).
test_conditions: Train on antenna reference angles (integers in 0-180 degrees; 10 random angles for Twin DQN); test on different unseen angles, zero-shot, no fine-tuning (pp. 11, 13).
baselines: GRU (beam prediction); Double DQN; non-learned Benchmark 1 (CSI-RS to six neighbors) and Benchmark 2 (sweep when SNR below 2.5 dB) (pp. 11, 13).
metrics: Beam prediction accuracy, average reward as data rate (bits/s/Hz), SNR against optimal-beam upper bound, share of resources used by CSI-RS (pp. 12-14).
complexity: GRNN has 3K=60 parameters versus 32,850 for GRU; storage O(3K), compute O(NC^2); inference 4.98 ms (GRNN) and 23.8 ms (Twin DQN) on CPU (pp. 7, 8, 11, 14).

title: MIMO-ODDM Signal Detection: A Spatial-Based Generative Adversarial Network Approach
q1_support: p. 9: "the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) tapped delay line-C (TDL-C) model [35], to build up the MIMO-ODDM system".

function: MIMO-ODDM signal detection: a spatial-based GAN (AMFG generator, SAMD discriminator) recovers transmitted delay-Doppler symbols from received signals, with transfer-learning updating (TAU) (pp. 1-2, 5).
system: MIMO-ODDM, 3x3 antennas with half-wavelength ULA, 4QAM, 3.5 GHz carrier, 300 km/h, 8 paths, N=64, M=128; no RIS (pp. 9-10, Table I).
method: Spatial-based GAN (attention generator with six-directional LSTM, attention discriminator), supervised offline training with L1 plus adversarial loss; transfer-learning update (TAU) fine-tunes one block (pp. 5-9).
data_channel: Simulated 3GPP TDL-C channel (ref. [35]), random delay and Doppler indices, 8 paths; labelled dataset of 10^6 samples (15625 ODDM symbols), 60/40 train/test split (pp. 9-10).

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Performance Optimization of RIS-Assisted Communications: Framework Design and Application to Energy Efficiency Maximization of Systems With RSMA
q1_support: p. 5: "components representing outdoor conditions, can be modeled as [34]"; p. 10: "following the 5G path loss model [43]". Custom statistical simulator; no 3GPP TR 38.901 profile, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is used.
q2_support: p. 10: "The following parameters were considered for the RIS-assisted RSMA communication system: N = 4, κ = 2, Nuser = 2, NTx = 2". Fig. 6 (p. 12) varies only the transmit SNR; no other scenario, size or band is tested.

function: Jointly optimizes BS transmit precoding and discrete RIS phase shifts to maximize energy efficiency of RIS-assisted RSMA, using two alternating quantum-circuit learning models (pp. 1, 7).
system: Downlink one-layer RSMA, BS with 2 antennas, 2 single-antenna users, reflecting single-connected RIS with N=4 elements and 10-bit discrete phases; carrier frequency not stated (pp. 4, 10).
method: Two variational quantum circuits with reduced-input encoding, unsupervised energy-efficiency loss, parameter-shift gradient descent, trained alternately (precoder, then RIS); run with IBM Qiskit (pp. 7-11).
data_channel: Custom simulation: LoS plus NLoS BS-RIS channel and LoS RIS-user channel after [34], 5G path-loss model [43], shadow fading, random angles; no dataset (pp. 5, 10).

baselines: Non-learned: conventional matched-filter precoding with cosine-similarity RIS phases; random precoding and random RIS phases. Learned: alternative quantum circuit model (QCNN-style, ref. [46]) (pp. 11-13).
metrics: Energy efficiency (bps/Hz/J) versus transmit SNR; training loss versus iteration (convergence); qubit counts; complexity order of encoding (pp. 11-12).
complexity: Encoding stage O(N) for quantum reduced-input versus O((Nuser+NTx)N) for classical input layer; qubits needed Nuser+Nreduce+N (RIS model) and Nuser+Nreduce+NTx (precoder) (pp. 11-12).

[46], p. 11 footnote 14) as the learned baseline; it shares the unsupervised framework of Algorithm 1, so the reviewer should confirm it is not a variant of the proposed model. q4 rests on the encoding-stage complexity and qubit counts only, not on a full-method analysis. Very small setup (4 RIS elements, 2 users).

title: Deep Reciprocity Calibration for TDD mmWave Massive MIMO Systems Toward 6G
q1_support: p. 9: "we employ the extended Saleh-Valenzuela model to simulate the mmWave channel"; p. 3: "we adopt the extended Saleh-Valenzuela geometric model [28]". Custom simulator with a textbook model; no 3GPP, QuaDRiGa, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.

title: Joint Optimization of Trajectory Control, Resource Allocation, and User Association Based on DRL for Multi-Fixed-Wing UAV Networks
q1_support: p. 4: "it is more accurate to adopt the Rician fading model"; custom Rician air-ground model with constants from [28], [34] (p. 10); no 3GPP, measured or ray-tracing channel is used.

title: Joint User Association, Interference Cancellation, and Power Control for Multi-IRS Assisted UAV Communications
function: above_phy: the only learned part (inverse soft-Q agent) decides the multi-IRS multi-user association (p. 6); trajectory, SIC order and power are solved by SCA.
first_notes: Reason above_phy. p. 1 abstract: 'We first propose an inverse soft-Q learning-based algorithm to optimize multi-IRS multi-user association. Then, SCA and Dinkelbach-based algorithm are leveraged to optimize UAV trajectory followed by the optimization of SIC decoding order scheduling and power allocation.' p. 6: 'we propose a user association algorithm based on inverse soft-Q learning'; the agent action is the binary association alpha (p. 6). The RIS phase shifts are a closed-form rule (Theorem 1, eq. 10, p. 4). The trajectory is solved by SCA and Dinkelbach, and the SIC order and power by penalty-based SCA, both with CVX (pp. 7 and 9), so no learned component sets a physical-layer variable (power, beams or RIS phases). Paper title matches the DOI (Ning et al., multi-IRS assisted UAV communications).
second_notes: Reason above_phy. p. 1: "an inverse soft-Q learning-based algorithm to optimize multi-IRS multi-user association. Then, SCA and Dinkelbach-based algorithm are leveraged to optimize UAV trajectory followed by the optimization of SIC decoding order scheduling and power allocation". p. 6: the agent's action A[t] is only the binary association alpha and its state is the UAV position ("define action A[t] ... to represent binary variable alpha chosen by the agent"). The RIS phase shifts follow a closed-form optimal strategy (p. 4, eq. (10), Theorem 1), so no learned component sets the RIS phases, the power, or any beam of the aerial link, and the learning acts on user association, which the instructions list above the physical layer. Not no_learning: learning is a core part of the proposed AISLE method, not a motivation or a baseline. For the reviewer to confirm: the association also fixes how the rows of each IRS are split among its users (p. 3, J_{s,i}[t] = J_b divided by the number of users served), which could be read as allocating reflecting resources of an aerial link; I kept user association because the paper names and formulates it so (title, p. 6 Section III.A). The PDF is arXiv:2312.04786v1 and matches the DOI (same title and authors in the DOI metadata).

(15)) and there is no receive beamformer, so the devices and the PS each have one antenna; y is a vector only because it carries the d entries of the gradient. [33]), and the simulation settings (p. 11) and figure legends (pp. 10-12, checked on the page images) vary only power, quantization bits, CSI accuracy rho, truncation threshold, number of devices, and the sampling scheme. title: Over-the-Air Federated Learning in MIMO Cloud Radio Access Networks

metrics: Test accuracy versus training round on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10; simulation time per communication round (Table II) (pp. 12-13).

Table I and Table II were not in the extracted text, so they were read from the page images of pp. 11 and 13 (NT=3, NR=8, alpha=3.8, power 5 W, Delta=30 m, noise -70 dBm; times per round). Why above_phy: the action of the DDQN agent is the 'price level decision' (p. 7, Eq. 11), its state is price and utility (Eq. 10) and its reward is revenue (Eq. 12). Blockchain-driven FL aggregates the pricing models digitally (pp. 8-9, Algorithm 2), not over the air. The uplink power-control level is adjusted by satellite operators under the reputation rule (p. 8: 'adjust the power control level'), so it is not an action of the learned agent. No link metric is evaluated: results are reward, price and revenue (pp. 11-14, Figs. 7-10). If the reviewer reads either point the other way, the work falls in area 6 (single-antenna links are admitted) with q1=0 (custom LEO simulator, p. 12), q2=0, q3=0 (the only learned baseline is plain DDQN, a variant of the proposed method, Fig. 10, pp. 13-14), q4=1 (Section IV-E, p. 10: O(KE sum L_i L_i+1)), q5=0.

The learned element is a DDQN per satellite, aggregated by blockchain-driven FL, and it sets the price of leased spectrum to maximize revenue. p. 7: "δs denotes the price level decision" (the state is price and utility, Eq. 10, and the reward is the utility change, Eq. 12). p. 1: "to learn a revenue-maximizing pricing scheme". Spectrum pricing is a market and network-management decision above the PHY. Power control is credited to the non-learned reputation mechanism. p. 1: "reputation-based blockchain which is used in the global model aggregation phase of FL to optimize the power control". The power level also works as an access threshold. p. 6: "if the required transmit power of a terrestrial user is bigger than the power control of the LEO satellite, then that user will not select this satellite's spectrum to lease". Results report only reward, price, and revenue (Section V, Figs. 7-10, pp. 11-14). For the reviewer: Algorithm 1 (p. 7) lets the action "change the price of the spectrum or the control level of power", and p. 8 says the DDQN searches "the optimal spectrum price and power control". V-A into an iterative Bayesian learning framework.' p. 10: 'directly optimizing the parameter estimates based on the observed data'. p. 1: 'employs expectation-maximization (EM) procedure to calculate the channel posterior distribution in the E step, and natural gradient descent algorithm to calculate the prior parameters in the M step'. p. 11, Algorithm 1 (read from the page image): input y_q, hyperparameters initialized to zero, E and M steps repeated until convergence or N_max; 'which runs at each AP independently'. p. 14: 'We fix the parameters for the proposed ConvBL algorithm as follows' (d = 10, step size 10^-2, 'maximum number of EM iterations Nmax = 100'). title: Generating High Dimensional User-Specific Wireless Channels Using Diffusion Models
q1_support: p. 8: "Berlin urban macro LOS scenario using the QuaDRiGa simulator [40]". The beam-alignment experiment uses DeepMIMO (p. 13: "we use the DeepMIMO dataset [13] to ensure site-specificity").

The PDF is the arXiv version 2409.03924v2, read as preprint.

title: Delay Deterministic Cell-Free MIMO Transmission via Safety Reinforcement Learning
function: Excluded as above_phy: the learned safety-RL (CUP) policy outputs user weights for rate scheduling from buffer and delay states (p. 3); the precoder itself is the classical WMMSE (p. 9).
first_notes: Reason above_phy. p. 1: 'rate scheduling via a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP), and instantaneous precoding through weighted sum-rate (WSR) maximization'. p. 3: the RL 'derive[s] user weights (action) reflecting priority in user rate scheduling, rather than high-dimensional beamforming matrices'. p. 8: the policy state is buffer delay and traffic bins plus the CSIT norm, and at inference 'only the policy network works, deriving the user weights'. p. 9-10: the precoder is computed by the non-learned WMMSE (Algorithm 3). p. 6: the WMMSE solution gives the bits per user 'before medium access control (MAC) executes FIFO scheduling', and the updated buffer drives the next weights. Borderline case: if the reviewer counts the learned weights as part of the precoder design, the area would be 3 and the marks q1 0 (custom Rayleigh simulator, p. 10), q2 0 (traffic sweep trained and tested per condition, p. 13), q3 0 (only learned baseline 'penalty' is a variant of CUP, p. 10), q4 1 (O(L_WMMSE,max N_bi U K Nt^3) and about 5,000 policy parameters, p. 10), q5 0 (no release).
second_notes: Reason above_phy. p. 3: the CUP agent derives "user weights (action) reflecting priority in user rate scheduling, rather than high-dimensional beamforming matrices". p. 1: "a safety reinforcement learning-based algorithm to optimize rate scheduling by allocating user weights, and a weighted minimum mean squared error (WMMSE) algorithm to solve the WSR maximization". p. 6: Section IV is "Data-Driven Safety-RL-Based User Weight Scheduling", and Algorithm 1 computes the precoders with the WMMSE of Algorithm 3 (p. 10), which has closed-form updates and no trained parameters. p. 11: the baselines EDF, MTF and equal weights are scheduling rules feeding the same WMMSE ("All schemes generate user weights as output to the WMMSE algorithm 3"), and the main metrics are delay jitter and delay violation ratio (p. 12). No physical-layer decision is learned, so it is not a joint physical-layer and scheduling design; no_learning not used because learning is the core of the method. Reviewer may check whether learned WSR user weights should count as learned precoding (area 3).

title: User-Centric Beam-Delay Alignment Transmission for Low-Altitude Coverage via Wideband Cell-Free Massive MIMO
q1_support: p. 3: "Salen-Valenzula is adopted in this paper". Custom Saleh-Valenzuela simulator; no 3GPP, DeepMIMO, or measured channel is used.
q2_support: p. 11: "The training hyperparameters are as follows: 0.002 for learning rate, 0.09 for penalty coefficient and 0.5 for dropout in the SCTConv layers and 200 for training epochs." Missing: the training data and any test in conditions not used for training; the results for 20, 30, and 40 UAVs (pp. 11-13) do not say the GCN was trained on another setting.

q4_support: p. 11: "The complexity in APs can be expressed as O(K^2 N)" and "The complexity of GCN, permutation and the second block of nested loops are O(K^2P^2), O(KP log KP) and O(κN_D KP)".

function: Selects the semi-synchronized path set, i.e., which UAV multipaths each AP serves with analog beams and delays, by GCN maximal-clique detection for asynchronous cooperative beamforming (pp. 3, 10).
system: Wideband mmWave cell-free massive MIMO downlink: 18 APs, 128-antenna ULA, 10 RF chains, analog delay modules; 20-40 single-antenna UAVs; no RIS; carrier frequency not stated (pp. 3, 11).
method: Geometric scattering GCN from [41] (linear input layer, 3 SCTConv layers, two linear layers), unsupervised training with the label-free clique loss (36) for 200 epochs (pp. 10-11).
data_channel: Simulated Saleh-Valenzuela mmWave multipath channel (3 paths, LoS and NLoS, propagation delays) over a 1 km x 1 km area; GCN training data not described (pp. 3, 11).
test_conditions: Training conditions not described beyond hyperparameters; tests with 20, 30, and 40 UAVs and 32 to 256 antennas, without saying whether the GCN is retrained (pp. 11-13).
baselines: Non-learned only: uniform-power BDAT, the hybrid delay hybrid beamforming architecture of Fig. 5, and the Bron-Kerbosch maximal clique list; no learned baseline (pp. 11-13).
metrics: Per-UE spectral efficiency CDF, energy efficiency and transmit power CDFs, and CDF of the selected clique index ratio against the Bron-Kerbosch list (pp. 11-13).
complexity: AP side O(K^2 N); GCN O(K^2 P^2); Algorithm 2 O(K^2 P^2); centralized power optimization O(-log(eps) L^3 K^3); fronthaul overhead L N_D^2 + L N_D + K (p. 11).
first_notes: Reason above_phy (user association). p. 3: 'Based on a given association strategy, the optimal asynchronous cooperative beamforming method is derived analytically'; the SSP-Set strategy is 'proposed to select serving user paths', using a GCN that 'uses the delay compensation as input and outputs the maximal clique probability'. p. 4: alpha_lkp says whether AP l serves UE k on path p. p. 6 and p. 10: precoders, delays and power come from closed forms, bisection and Algorithm 1, with no learned part. p. 10: the GCN only 'refines the initial feature' of delay compensation for maximal clique detection, replacing Bron-Kerbosch (p. 13). The GCN is auxiliary to an analytical design, so the reviewer may prefer no_learning, and the exclusion holds either way. Borderline case: if the reviewer reads the path selection as beam selection, the area would be 3 and the marks q1 0 (custom Saleh-Valenzuela channel, p. 3), q2 0 (K and N sweeps without stated training split, pp. 11-12), q3 0 (only classical Bron-Kerbosch compared, p. 13), q4 1 (O(K^2 P^2) and O(K^2 N) at the APs, p. 11), q5 0 (no release).
second_notes: Included: the GCN has trained parameters (p. 10: "Θ in (35) is the learnable parameter set in GCN") and selects the SSP-Set, i.e., the serving indicators of the precoding problem (11) (p. 4: "an indicator implying whether l-th AP serves k-th UE in p-th path"; p. 5). The paper calls the SSP-Set an "association strategy" (p. 3), but it chooses which paths get analog beams so as to avoid ICI and ISI, so I read it as beam selection (area 3), not above_phy. Area 3 rather than 6: the UAVs are UEs of a terrestrial cell-free network (p. 3: "UAVs in our system are UES instead of base stations or relays"), and the paper sets LEO and HAPS aside (pp. 1-2); reviewer may confirm whether ground-to-UAV links count as aerial links of area 6. title: Secrecy Sum Rate Maximization in UAV-IRS Assisted Networks With Credit-Aware Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
q1_support: p. 4: "We model the above channels as the Rician channel"; p. 11: "ρ = 20 dB, ξ = 2.2, β = 10 dB". Custom Rician simulator, with no 3GPP model, ray-tracing set or measurement.
q2_support: p. 12: "cumulative average security rate of users for the six algorithms versus the number of UAVs". Missing: the paper never says a trained policy is tested on a configuration unseen in training or adapted; p. 13 imperfect CSI is only a CSI-error sweep.
q3_support: p. 11: MASAC-TR agents "optimise their strategies directly using team reward as the learning reward"; the three MASAC baselines are the proposal without credit allocation or constraint. p. 12: "random phase shift (RPS)" is non-learned. Missing: no earlier published learned method is compared.
q4_support: p. 10: "the complexity of the training process of the scheme is OT = O(Nepi T ((N + M )N ! + |B|(OP + OR + OC )))".

function: Jointly learns the phase-shift matrices and flight displacements of multiple UAV-IRS relays to maximize the downlink secrecy sum rate against eavesdroppers (p. 5, p. 6).
system: BS with K=20 antennas, 20 single-antenna users, 2 single-antenna eavesdroppers, 3 reflecting (passive) UAV-IRS with 15 elements each; direct link blocked; no frequency band stated (pp. 3-4, 11).
method: Multi-agent soft actor-critic (PD-CMASAC) with three-layer MLP actor and critics, centralized training with distributed execution, Shapley-value credit rewards, primal-dual constraint; online reinforcement learning (pp. 7-11).
data_channel: Custom simulator: Rician channels with path loss (rho 20 dB, xi 2.2, beta 10 dB), 1 km square, Gaussian-Markov user mobility; no dataset or measurements (pp. 4, 11).
test_conditions: Policies trained online over episodes in the same simulated setting (Fig. 3); results vary UAV, IRS-element and user numbers and CSI error, with no stated train-test split (pp. 11-13).
baselines: MASAC-TR, MASAC-IR, MASAC-RS (learned variants of the proposal); RPS random phase and FUP fixed position, each with the other variable learned by PD-CMASAC (pp. 11-12).
metrics: Cumulative average and sum secrecy rate (bit/s/Hz), cumulative cost of non-cooperative behaviour, Jain fairness index (pp. 11-13).
complexity: Training order O(N_epi T((N+M)N! + |B|(O_P+O_R+O_C))), individual-reward step O((M+N)N!); no measured runtime (p. 10).

Channel estimation is least squares over dominant rays (p. 8, Algorithms 1 and 2) and passive beamforming is a continuous relaxation solved per realization with Adam (p. 10); no network is trained for the estimation or the beamforming step, and all rate baselines are non-learned: Random, Best Sounding, Group-Opt, Phased Array (p. 11). If the reviewer counts the DNN surrogate as a learned physical-layer component, the closest area is 3 and the marks would be q1=1 (p. 10: 3GPP ray-tracing model of TS 38.901, Indoor-Office), q2=0, q3=0, q4=1 (Table II, p. 7: FLOPs and parameters), q5=0 (no code or data link).
second_notes: PDF is arXiv:2510.20354v1; its title and authors match the Crossref record of the DOI (IEEE Trans. Wireless Commun., 2026). Eligibility is borderline on check 3 (no_learning): the only learned component is a supervised DNN that approximates the pixel-RIS element response nu(phi_in, phi_out; l) (pp. 5-6). Channel estimation (LS and grid search, Algorithms 1-2, pp. 8-10) and passive beamforming (softmax relaxation optimized per instance with Adam, no training, p. 10) are model-based. I include it because the DNN output enters the regressors of the cascaded-channel estimator, the channel prediction for RIS states never sounded, and the beamforming objective (p. 12: "We introduced a DNN to model the RIS response function"). The reviewer should confirm that a learned model of the RIS response counts as a learned component that performs the function; if not, exclude as no_learning (p. 8, p. 10). Area: the solution addresses channel estimation (area 2) and passive beamforming (area 3) together. The main metric is the sum rate (p. 5: "The primary objective of this paper is to configure an appropriate RIS state st to maximize the sum rate"; Figs. 11-12 are the only comparisons with baselines), so area 3. Area 2 is the alternative if the DNN is read as channel synthesis. q1: the DNN is trained on samples of the RIS element response (the paper does not say whether these come from EM simulation or measurement of the prototype in [4]), not on channels. All channel-dependent evaluation uses 3GPP 38.901 Sec. 7.5, Indoor-Office (Table 7.5-6) with the K-factor set to 3 dB. The paper calls this the "3GPP ray-tracing model" and cites it as TS 38.901 v18.0.0; Sec. 7.5 is the fast-fading model of TR 38.901. The system model is also stated to follow "the 3GPP channel model [37, Section 7]" (p. 4). The paper does not say whether the DNN or the kernel approximation is used in the simulations of Figs. 10-12. q2: the channel-prediction NMSE uses "100 random RIS configurations not observed during the channel sounding phases" (p. 11). That tests the model-based estimator, not the trained DNN, and the DNN does not depend on M or K, so the two setups are not a new condition for it. q3: the channel-estimation NMSE (Fig. 10) has no baseline at all.
published_notes: Excluded as no_learning (borderline call, flagged for the reviewer). The only learned element is a DNN, with a Legendre-kernel alternative, that approximates the 4D response of one pixel-RIS element; it is trained by supervised NMSE regression on 10^7 angle pairs per state (p. 6: "train the weights" ... "to minimize the approximation NMSE"). It models RIS hardware and is independent of the propagation (p. 4: "determined solely by the structure of the pixel RIS element"). The physical-layer functions are not learned. Section IV is "MODEL-BASED CHANNEL ESTIMATION" (p. 6), an LS and grid-search procedure (Algorithm 1 on p. 8, Algorithm 2 on p. 10). Passive beamforming relaxes the discrete states and runs Adam on each instance (p. 10: "We solve P(A-3) by utilizing Adam optimizer [39] in PyTorch"). The simulation baselines Random, Best Sounding, Group-Opt and Phased Array (p. 10-11) are all non-learned, and the text never says which approximator feeds the estimator in the simulation. If the reviewer counts the DNN surrogate as a learned component, the alternative reason is function (RIS element response modelling, none of the seven areas), so the work stays excluded either way.

title: UAV Tracking Using Channel-Anomaly-Based Deep Learning in ISAC Systems
function: Excluded (function): the learned network detects a UAV and predicts its 3D trajectory from uplink CSI, which is target positioning and tracking; it learns no beams, waveforms or resources. p. 9: "a sequence of Lo position estimates"; p. 13: "Overall positioning error has a median of approximately 4.5 m".
first_notes: Reason: function (Step 1, rule 5), positioning or localization is an excluded function. p. 1 abstract: the scheme "passively detects uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) by exploiting channel anomalies" in the first Fresnel zone, using a two-stage DL framework (appearance-time detector, then a BiLSTM with attention for trajectory prediction; pp. 7-9). The network outputs the 3D UAV coordinates (p. 9) and is scored by positioning RMSE against a particle filter (pp. 12-13). It does not design beams, waveforms or resources for sensing and communication (area 5); the communication link is not changed by the learned model. Channel estimation is least squares, not learned (p. 5: "The BS recovers the channel via least squares estimation"). Angle estimation is classical spatially smoothed 2D-MUSIC with a closed-form CRLB (pp. 10-11) and "does not require DL training" (p. 15). Learning is present, so no_learning does not apply; the learning acts on CSI of the physical layer to track a non-cooperative target, not on UAV control, so above_phy does not apply. Setup for the reviewer: single-antenna UEs, 10x10 URA base station, no RIS, 2.6 GHz, own geometry-based Rician simulator (pp. 2, 5, 11). A reviewer may confirm that passive sensing on the communication uplink is not area 5.
second_notes: Reason function, first applicable code: research article whose learned CNN-LSTM and BiLSTM-attention networks act on physical-layer CSI. p. 7: "First, a lightweight network monitors CSI power features continuously to detect UAV presence", then estimates and predicts the UAV trajectory (target sensing/positioning). Area 5 does not fit: no learned beam, waveform, or resource design; the channel itself is estimated by LS (p. 5) and the angles by non-learned 2D-MUSIC (p. 10). above_phy does not apply: the UAV trajectory is estimated, not controlled.

title: Optimal Transceiver Design in Over-the-Air Federated Distillation
q1_support: p. 7: "The channel coefficient is modelled by the small scale fading multiplied by the square root of the path loss": IID Gaussian fading with free-space path loss; custom simulator, no 3GPP, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data.
q2_support: p. 7: "we further devise the following IID and non-IID dataset settings for the CIFAR-10 dataset"; p. 8: sweeps of distillation weight, antennas and CSI error; each run trains its own model. No model is tested in an unseen scenario, band or dataset.
q3_support: p. 9: "(Over-the-air FD with) MSE Minimization [11]" and "(Over-the-air FL with) 90%-Sparse Rate [9]" are earlier published designs, with "the proposed algorithm achieves a higher performance than the MSE minimization benchmark" (testing accuracy); "Uniform Beamforming" is the non-learned baseline.
q4_support: p. 7: "the overall computational complexity of obtaining the optimal" transceivers per FD round is O(N^3 + M); footnote 4: "Algorithm 1 is 0.12s" average run time per round. Cost of the transceiver design, not the model size.
q5_support: p. 7: "We simulate an image classification task on ResNet-18 over the FMNIST and CIFAR-10 dataset": public datasets of the learning task only; channels are simulated; no code or data link is given in the paper.
function: Transceiver design for over-the-air aggregation of local soft predictions in federated distillation: device transmit power, PS estimator scalars and receive beamforming, maximizing the convergence rate (p. 1, p. 3).
system: PS with 5 antennas (5 to 100 in sweep), 50 single-antenna devices (100 for ViT), analog over-the-air aggregation, block fading; no RIS; 915 MHz (p. 7-10).
method: Federated distillation: devices train ResNet-18 or ViT-B/16 by gradient descent with a soft-prediction distillation regularizer; transceiver by closed form and semidefinite relaxation, not learned (p. 3, p. 7-10).
data_channel: Simulated IID Gaussian small-scale fading with path loss exponent 4; FMNIST, CIFAR-10 (IID and Dirichlet non-IID), Oxford Flowers (ViT) datasets (p. 7, p. 10).
test_conditions: Separate training runs, tested on held-out sets: FMNIST 400 rounds, CIFAR-10 200 rounds; IID and non-IID splits; sweeps of distillation weight, antennas, CSI error (p. 7-10).
baselines: Error-free FD, error-free FedAvg, uniform beamforming, orthogonal channels, MSE minimization [11], sparsified over-the-air FL [9], pruned and quantized over-the-air FL [15], digital OFDMA FD [38] (p. 9-11).
metrics: Global testing accuracy versus rounds, total time and uplink time; analytical convergence gap; training and distillation loss; eigenvalues of the relaxed beamformer; run time per round (p. 7-10).
complexity: Algorithm 1 per round O(N^3 + M) (interior point plus eigendecomposition O(N^2.376)); measured average run time 0.12 s per round (p. 7).
openness: none; no code or data link, only public FMNIST, CIFAR-10 and Oxford Flowers datasets (p. 7, p. 10).
first_notes: Preprint arXiv:2507.15256v1, titled 'Optimal Transceiver Design in Over-the-Air Federated Distillation'; the DOI cannot be checked against the title from the PDF alone.
